#5167. Morning Minute: Nvidia Beats, Board Says ‘No’ on Jensen

Morning Minute: Nvidia Beats, Board Says ‘No’ on Jensen

Morning Minute is a daily newsletter written by Tyler Warner. The analysis and opinions expressed are his own and do not necessarily reflect those of Decrypt. And check out our daily news show 'FOMO HOUR' covering all of the top stories and market action.

🖥️ Nvidia Beats, Board Says ‘No’ on Jensen

Six days after Jensen Huang resigned as CEO of the company he co-founded 33 years ago, Nvidia delivered the best quarter in its history. And told him he isn’t coming back.

Fourth-quarter guidance came in at $130 billion against the $125.3 billion Wall Street wanted, with China assumed at zero.

And the CFO raised their 2028 revenue outlook to 75% year-over-year growth.

Then board chair Harvey Jones got on the call and said it plainly. “The Nvidia board does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO.” The directors unanimously accepted his resignation, and Jones declined to answer anything about the circumstances or the independent investigation still running.

Huang had publicly offered to come back hours earlier, saying he would do it if directors believed it served shareholders and employees. Trump and Elon Musk both backed the idea. A petition passed 182,000 signatures including nearly 9,000 self-identified Nvidia employees. None of it moved the room.

Nvidia has hired Heidrick & Struggles to run the permanent search. Colette Kress stays interim CEO while remaining CFO, with Jones saying the board has “every confidence in Colette’s leadership, integrity and ability to deliver.” The board also created a National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee, chaired by director Suzanne Nora Johnson, to receive reports from the company’s national security and trade compliance teams.

And after all of that—the stock rose about 3%.

A 6% revenue beat, guidance $5 billion above consensus, a new product cycle shipping, and the market gave it two percent. Shares sit roughly 35% below their October peak near $240. Nvidia perps on Hyperliquid were doing nearly a billion dollars of daily volume through the week, bouncing off $150 before settling near $162.

As for impact on the broader AI trade, Nvidia proved AI demand is not collapsing. You cannot manufacture $107.6 billion of data center revenue, and margins at 74.8% mean nobody is discounting to move product. The demand-collapse thesis died on Tuesday.

Two details do belong to the bears though. Growth is decelerating from 103% to roughly 77% once you strip the extra week out of Q4 guidance. And gross margin guides down about three points, from 74.8% to between 71% and 72%. Slowing growth plus compressing margins is how multiples come down regardless of how big the absolute numbers get.

The honest read is that the AI business is fine and the AI trade has stopped responding to it. For crypto that matters more than it should, because the correlation that dragged Bitcoin from $87,000 to the low $60s over six weeks ran through this exact trade.

Now we wait for the Fed on December 9 and insight into the 2027 rate hike cycle (or lack thereof) to determine the likely near-term fate.

#5166. Ethereum targets December Glamsterdam test despite 200 findings that could delay upgrade

Developers are leaning toward retaining the upgrade's existing rules, potentially clearing the way for a January mainnet launch after an earlier test was postponed.

Ethereum developers are leaning toward retaining Glamsterdam's gas rules despite 200 findings that could disrupt existing smart contracts.

During a Nov. 19 core developers meeting, participants expressed broad support for proceeding with the current specifications rather than introducing changes that could push the network upgrade into April or May 2027.

Developers tentatively targeted the week of Dec. 14 for testing on Ethereum's Hoodi network, potentially allowing a mainnet activation as early as mid-January. However, the schedule remains unconfirmed as teams address compatibility problems affecting existing applications.

Glamsterdam is designed to significantly expand Ethereum's capacity, potentially increasing its block gas limit from 60 million to 200 million, a more than threefold increase.

According to Ethereum research firm Ethlabs, the expansion would give applications more room to operate directly on Ethereum's main network while reducing congestion and transaction fees during periods of heavy demand.

However, achieving that capacity requires changing how Ethereum charges for certain computing operations and data storage.

Two proposals, EIP-8037 and EIP-8038, introduce new gas pricing and accounting rules that could invalidate assumptions built into existing smart contracts.

A ChainSecurity assessment identified 200 compatibility findings across its investigations and work coordinated by the Ethereum Foundation.

Of these, three were classified as high severity, 30 as medium and 167 as low. None was rated critical.

The assessment identified potential disruptions affecting bridges, exchanges, wallets, staking platforms, governance systems, and other infrastructure supporting Ethereum applications.

Most findings can be addressed through configuration changes, but 24 require smart contract upgrades or migrations. Potential consequences include interrupted operations, locked funds, and errors in reward accounting.

The problem stems partly from applications that rely on fixed gas allowances to perform specific operations. Under Glamsterdam's proposed rules, those allowances may no longer be sufficient to complete the same work.

Recent Juicebox V6 simulations demonstrated the consequences. Some transactions were recorded as successful even though internal payments failed or were skipped under the tested rules.

Ethlabs acknowledged that changing gas prices is necessary to support Ethereum's expansion but distinguished those changes from accounting modifications that introduced unexpected behavior.

The research firm argued that protocol developers must convince application developers of the upgrade's safety.

Despite the findings, Ethereum developers remain divided over whether modifying Glamsterdam's specifications would meaningfully improve compatibility.

The Besu client team advocated exploring a targeted revision to EIP-8037 to preserve existing smart contract behavior.

However, Ansgar Dietrichs and several other developers questioned whether a narrow adjustment would resolve enough problems to justify additional testing and development delays.

Marius van der Wijden also warned that changing how gas refunds are handled could disrupt contracts that depend on receiving those refunds during transaction execution.

The disagreement leaves developers choosing between allowing affected applications time to adjust to the existing specifications and redesigning parts of the upgrade to preserve more of their current behavior.

The Ethereum Foundation, alongside security researchers, has contacted more than 50 affected companies. During the meeting, Rahul reported that high-impact projects had completed or were expected to complete fixes by mid-December.

Other affected projects reported remediation schedules extending to Jan. 10, making mid-January the earliest viable mainnet activation window without specification changes.

A late-January or early-February rollout was also discussed as a more realistic possibility.

However, Dietrichs outlined substantially longer timelines if developers postpone their decision to investigate alternative rules.

Waiting until January to decide whether to retain the existing specifications could push activation into late February or early March. Adopting specification changes then could extend the rollout to April or May.

Such delays would also affect Ethereum's broader upgrade schedule, including preparations for Hegotá, which developers are discussing in connection with the network's post-quantum security transition.

The competing priorities have strengthened support for maintaining Glamsterdam's current design.

Developers are now considering a Hoodi activation around Dec. 16 or 17, after an earlier October test was postponed over compatibility concerns.

#5164. Movie2K Defendant Could Hand Over 40,000 Bitcoin to End Trial—and Stay a Billionaire

Movie2K Defendant Could Hand Over 40,000 Bitcoin to End Trial—and Stay a Billionaire

The alleged operator of defunct movie piracy site Movie2K could walk away from his trial in Germany and remain a billionaire, under a deal offered by the judge in the case.

The presiding judge at the Leipzig Regional Court has offered to drop tax evasion and money laundering charges against the 43-year-old main defendant if he hands over 40,000 BTC, public broadcaster MDR reported last week. He would also have to pay €38 million ($42 million) in compensation for potential victims, according to MDR.

Saxony's Office of the Public Prosecutor General confirmed the offer to news agency dpa, tech outlet heise reported on Tuesday. The 40,000 BTC would be worth around €2.36 billion ($2.6 billion) at current prices, according to heise.

But prosecutors believe the defendant holds a total of about 56,000 BTC. If he accepts, he could keep around 16,000 BTC, worth roughly €940 million ($1 billion) today and more than €1 billion when the offer was made.

A co-defendant has been offered a deal to hand over 600 BTC and pay €17 million ($19 million), and his lawyer said she could accept it, according to MDR. The main defendant's lawyers are considering the offer. The trial resumes on December 3 and could end before Christmas.

Movie2K offered hundreds of thousands of pirated films before shutting down in 2013. Its operators made money from advertising and subscription traps, and invested much of it in Bitcoin when it traded far below today's prices.

The copyright violations are time-barred, so the trial, which began in February, has focused on money laundering and tax evasion. The judge has reportedly expressed doubts about proving some of the charges, in part because legally and illegally acquired Bitcoin may have been mixed in the defendant's accounts, heise reported.

The main defendant was arrested abroad in 2023, and in early 2024 handed over nearly 50,000 BTC. Authorities in Saxony sold the coins later that year, raising about €2.64 billion ($2.9 billion), which is held in a state judicial treasury account. The money still belongs to the defendant until there is a final ruling, according to heise. Germany's government was left holding less than $300 million in Bitcoin after the sales.

Blockchain analytics firm Arkham said last year that German authorities had failed to seize some 45,000 BTC linked to the site.

The offer comes days after German lawmakers approved new powers allowing customs officials to seize assets, including crypto, of doubtful origin without first opening a criminal case. Under that law, owners of significant assets would have to show they were lawfully obtained.

#5162. Bitcoin missed AI stocks’ 85% rally but could still face the fallout if the boom unravels

Bitcoin fell on 77% of major Nasdaq down days since January 2024, a pattern drawing attention as the Fed examines risks from AI-related debt and financing.

DWF Labs reported on Nov. 19 that Bitcoin fell on 77% of US trading days when QQQ, an ETF that tracks the Nasdaq-100, lost at least 1%.

The analysis covers the period from the start of US spot Bitcoin ETF trading on Jan. 11, 2024, through Nov. 13, 2026. DWF put Bitcoin’s average decline on large Nasdaq down days at about 2%.

In the Federal Reserve’s October meeting minutes, released Nov. 18, almost all participants discussed what could happen if returns on artificial intelligence investments disappointed. Most pointed to rapid growth in AI-related debt and the complex, opaque structures used to finance much of it.

From September 2025 through the end of the study’s data on Nov. 13, the iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) gained 85% while Bitcoin fell 39%, according to DWF Labs.

If an AI selloff spreads from chip stocks to the wider Nasdaq-100, Bitcoin’s record on those down days becomes more relevant than its trading during the chip rally.

At the Oct. 27-28 meeting, many participants discussed the potential consequences of AI-related assets losing value if investors became less confident about the returns.

A few noted that exposure was becoming concentrated among a small number of firms, raising questions about how the buildout was financed and what the projects themselves might earn.

Fed staff flagged two structures that could amplify losses if returns disappointed.

One was off-balance-sheet leases, which can leave firms committed to future payments that do not appear on their balance sheets. The other was circular financing among AI-related firms, which ties their funding to one another.

Investors who borrowed to buy assets might have to sell holdings to reduce their debt, while fund managers might also need to sell to meet withdrawals. In the most severe scenarios, sales by vehicles such as hedge funds, bond mutual funds and target-date funds could make it harder for markets to absorb trades.

Elevated asset valuations and hedge fund leverage were the biggest vulnerabilities in the staff assessment. Strong bank and household balance sheets offered a buffer against more severe outcomes, and several participants noted the staff’s finding that banks were well capitalized.

Some participants saw gaps in the picture, and several questioned whether supervisors had enough data on banks’ indirect exposure through nonbank institutions, such as credit lines to private credit funds.

The minutes describe a stress scenario in which an asset-price decline compounds through financing commitments, leverage and the need to raise cash.

The connection for Bitcoin investors would depend on whether those pressures move beyond AI-related firms and pull down the wider market.

DWF Labs measured Bitcoin’s performance on days when a fund tracking the Nasdaq-100 dropped at least 1%.

The report found a similar pattern before US spot Bitcoin ETFs began trading. From 2020 until the January 2024 launch, Bitcoin fell on 74% of the Nasdaq-100 proxy’s large down days, and it fell on 77% from the launch through Nov. 13, 2026.

Yahoo Finance’s adjusted closes show 91 Bitcoin declines across 118 days when QQQ fell at least 1% in the latter period. Bitcoin’s average log return across all 118 days was -1.93%, including days when Bitcoin rose or held steady as well as days when it fell.

QQQ’s return runs from the prior US trading session’s close. Bitcoin’s return runs across consecutive calendar-day closes, with its daily candle ending at midnight UTC, three to four hours after the US stock market closes.

Closing prices alone don't capture the order of moves, and Bitcoin can keep moving for several hours after the US trading session ends, so the comparison includes part of that post-close window.

CryptoSlate compared QQQ and Bitcoin adjusted closes on the same dates using Yahoo Finance data.

Bitcoin closed lower on more than three quarters of the qualifying sessions.

Sessions qualified when QQQ’s daily log return was −1% or lower, regardless of cause. Bitcoin closes at midnight UTC, several hours after U.S. equities.

Use QQQ adjusted-close log returns on U.S. trading days and same-date BTC-USD adjusted-close log returns from Yahoo Finance. Filter at QQQ declines of at least 1%. Divide 91 Bitcoin declines by 118, rounded to 77.1%. The remaining 27 sessions equal 118 minus 91. Bar widths are proportional.

Sessions qualified when QQQ’s daily log return was −1% or lower, regardless of cause. Bitcoin closes at midnight UTC, several hours after U.S. equities.

CME Group research found that Bitcoin and US stocks often moved more closely together in periods of market stress. One possible explanation is the need for cash, since an investor reducing borrowing or covering losses can sell Bitcoin alongside stocks to raise it.

DWF’s results subtracted QQQ’s daily return from Bitcoin’s and SOXX’s returns. On that measure, the two had a correlation of negative 0.30 from March 2026 through the end of the sample. When chip stocks beat the Nasdaq-100 proxy, Bitcoin tended to lag it.

From September 2025 through Nov. 13, the iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) gained 85% and Bitcoin fell 39%.

A separate analysis by Block Scholes researcher Thahbib Rahman found that broader market moves explained part of a recent Bitcoin decline. His firm found little evidence that investors sold Bitcoin specifically to buy AI assets.

The Fed held rates in October, and almost all participants judged further increases likely under their baseline outlooks.

US consumer prices rose 0.4% in October from September, and the advance estimate showed nominal retail and food services sales up 0.2%, within its margin of error, while industrial production fell 0.4%.

In the Philadelphia Fed’s November manufacturing survey, regional activity fell to 6.3 from 20.9 as the prices-received index rose to 47.0, the highest since June 2022.

Investors should watch whether declines spread across the Nasdaq-100 and how Treasury yields and the Fed rate outlook respond.

A chip-sector drop with little effect on the index would signal Bitcoin differently than a selloff that reaches the rest of the market. Bitcoin’s response would show how closely it is moving with equities in that episode.

#5159. Bitcoin buyers face a trading issue as stablecoins just suffer their biggest supply drop since 2022

Market makers can advance stablecoins for institutional Bitcoin purchases and settle later against fund holdings, even as marketwide stablecoin supply falls $14.2 billion.

An institutional investor can ask a market maker to buy Bitcoin before the investor has turned tokenized fund shares into cash.

Greg Guttas, head of over-the-counter trading at Flowdesk, told CryptoSlate that the desk could pay with its own stablecoins and settle with the client later against the fund holding.

Securitize and Ethena opened a new route for fund holders on Nov. 12 with a facility for BlackRock’s USD Institutional Digital Liquidity Fund (BUIDL) that exchanges fund shares for stablecoins outside banking hours. That gives eligible investors a way to raise trading cash themselves.

In Guttas’s example, a dealer would supply the cash for the Bitcoin purchase upfront.

The question of what dealers can spend is sharper after a drop in stablecoin supply. Glassnode reported that aggregate stablecoin supply fell $14.2 billion in the 30 days through Nov. 9, the fastest contraction since June 2022.

The marketwide total leaves open how much an individual desk has on hand and what it would commit to a client’s trade.

Guttas described how an over-the-counter desk could handle a purchase for a client holding tokenized money-market fund shares:

“The market maker in that scenario could use their own stablecoin balances to buy the BTC immediately and then redeem the tokenized MM funds after the fact.”

That sequence would give the client time to settle using the fund position, while the dealer would spend the stablecoins first and wait for settlement to recover them. Until then, those funds would be unavailable for another purchase.

The longer it takes to turn fund shares into settlement cash, the longer the desk has to carry the exposure. Guttas said larger conversions can hit size limits, and weekends can complicate access.

In January 2025, QCP disclosed that it facilitated a six-month Bitcoin basis trade for Securitize Credit using BUIDL as collateral.

A basis trade aims to capture the difference between spot and futures prices, but QCP’s account leaves the funding currency for the Bitcoin leg and the settlement timing undisclosed.

The Securitize and Ethena facility works in both directions for BUIDL. Eligible investors can exchange their fund shares for supported stablecoins, including USDC, or use those stablecoins to acquire BUIDL.

That route can give a fund holder cash to trade on a weekend.

The facility opened with $50 million of inventory, split between $25 million in USDC and $25 million in BUIDL. Securitize said up to another $50 million may become available within about an hour as liquidity is used, subject to terms and availability, bringing the maximum facility capacity to $100 million.

The relevant starting figure for a holder seeking stablecoins at launch was the $25 million in USDC, while the BUIDL side of the inventory serves investors converting stablecoins into fund shares.

Circle’s USYC, a separate fund token restricted to eligible non-US investors, redeems into USDC in one block below its instant-redemption threshold, with per-block time varying by network.

Above that threshold, Circle lists same-day or next-day settlement, with separate arrangements available for additional immediate liquidity.

Katana CEO Matthew Fisher told CryptoSlate he looks at exchange balances, stablecoins posted as collateral in lending and perpetual futures markets, and how much traders borrow against them.

Those measures help show where stablecoins are being used for trading and leverage, but a balance on an exchange can sit there without becoming a Bitcoin order. Fisher advised watching the deployed number.

How large a trade an institution could finance depends on the dealer’s available inventory, the terms it offers, and how quickly the fund position can be converted into settlement cash. The arrangement would put existing stablecoins to work earlier in the trade.

#5157. Institutions are Piling Into Bitcoin ETFs, Pushing Holdings to a Record

Institutions returned to U.S. spot bitcoin exchange-traded products as net buyers in the third quarter, pushing their combined holdings to a record 356,491 BTC, according to a new report from Galaxy Research.

Investment managers that file Form 13F with the SEC added the equivalent o f 49,229 BTC, net of sales, between July 1 and Sept. 30. That is the most since the second quarter of 2025 and more than the 47,054 BTC they sold over the previous three quarters. The holdings were worth $29.78 billion at quarter-end prices.

Alex Thorn, Galaxy’s head of firmwide research, published the analysis Thursday. The buying came as bitcoin swung between a bear-market low of $57,717 on July 1 and a high of $87,397 on Sept. 21, and Galaxy said the accumulation continued through that range.

Half of the net addition came from advisors and wealth platforms, a group that includes registered investment advisors, wealth managers, wirehouses and broker-dealer platforms. The category reported 144,307 BTC, or 40.5% of all 13F-reported holdings, the highest share since the funds launched in January 2024.

Those firms have now been net buyers for nine straight quarters. Their holdings are 3.3 times their March 2024 level, and Galaxy said the group accounts for 100,003 of the 179,300 BTC that all filers have added since the second quarter of 2024.

Wirehouses drove the quarter. The category added a record 24,838 BTC, led by Wells Fargo at 14,636 BTC, Bank of America at 7,201 BTC and Morgan Stanley at 2,875 BTC.

Wells Fargo became the largest 13F holder for the first time. It reported 30,553 BTC, worth $2.55 billion, nearly double the 15,931 BTC it held on June 30, and passed Jane Street. No wealth platform had ranked first before, and Millennium Management had held the top spot in every quarter from early 2024 through the first quarter of 2026.

Hedge funds now hold 19.0% of 13F-reported holdings, down from 50.6% at the end of 2024. Basis and relative-value funds hold 34,053 BTC, far below their peak of 101,826 BTC, though they and macro funds were both buyers last quarter, adding 9,184 BTC and 10,492 BTC.

BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust accounts for two-thirds of the institutional position. Filers hold 232,453 BTC in the fund, or 65.2% of everything reported, and IBIT took 34,744 BTC of the quarter’s net 49,229 BTC.

Filers’ holdings of Grayscale’s GBTC fell for the 10th straight quarter, and the lower-fee Grayscale Bitcoin Mini Trust passed it for the first time. The number of managers holding a spot bitcoin fund rose by 191 to 2,166, the first increase after two quarters of decline.

Galaxy noted that a few large firms drove the gain. The 50 largest holders added a net 59,578 BTC, while all other managers combined were net sellers of 10,349 BTC. Form 13F filers hold 27.6% of the bitcoin in the funds, up from 24.8% on June 30.

The filings describe Sept. 30, and the picture has changed since. Galaxy said the funds’ bitcoin holdings have fallen by 38,531 BTC to 1,252,139 BTC as of Nov. 16, while the price of bitcoin dropped to $64,943 from $83,580. Bitcoin had traded above $81,500 as recently as Oct. 28.

A Form 13F covers only long positions at quarter-end and only accounts over which the manager has investment discretion. Short positions and most derivatives are not reported, so shares held by a market maker or basis fund may be hedged. Galaxy also believes client-directed brokerage accounts leave wealth-channel ownership understated.

How filers behaved during the recent decline will not be known until the next round of filings arrives in February.

#5156. 'It Speaks in Tongues That Only 6.2 Astra Understands': Why Early Testers Hate OpenAI’s New Model

'It Speaks in Tongues That Only 6.2 Astra Understands': Why Early Testers Hate OpenAI’s New Model

For an AI developer, hearing that your model is nice is always pretty good. But hearing your model is like a "sadistic shinigami that turns your life into a living hell," is a totally different thing.

OpenAI released GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol on Tuesday, promising smarter AI agents, better coding and impressive creative capabilities. Some of the developers who tested the models before launch had a rather different message: They're brilliant, frustrating and, in certain cases, almost impossible to work with.

The reaction quickly spilled across social media. AI engineer Hesam, who is very active in the AI community declared that “everyone agrees it’s the worst model OAI dropped.”

Developer and T3 Code creator Theo Browne published a lengthy letter to OpenAI following early testing. “I do not like 6.2 Astra. I would not choose this over Opus 5.5 for my work as a developer,” he wrote. He said OpenAI had fixed only a handful of the complaints he submitted.

“It speaks in tongues that only 6.2 Astra understands,” Theo wrote, calling its answers “the most unparsable outputs of any llm I've used this year,” referring to large language models. The complaint was as much about communication as capability: Astra could solve complex problems but struggled to explain what it had done or recognize when it was asking users questions they could not possibly answer.

In one experiment, Theo asked Astra to create a new level for Outer Wilds. Two hours into the project, the model declared itself blocked and asked: “does r24's reviewer write it's clips to 24_g521.mp4 or 24_p11.mp4?” The technical question was, from his perspective, incomprehensible and irrelevant to someone who had simply requested a playable level.

Things went worse in a code rewrite. Theo said he gave Astra seven days to improve the project; it landed no improvements and made the compiler 56% slower. Four more days yielded zero changes. “It runs in loops and goes nowhere,” he wrote.

This whole weird language issue is not isolated. For example, pseudonymous account, TokenGremlin, praised the model: “GPT-6.2 Astra is SOTA in Three.js, Blender, and 3D,” but said it “starts speaking an alien language during long workflows.”

Theo also described asking why worktrees were slow on one computer. Astra responded with four paragraphs about package-manager internals and cache behavior. The answer Theo said he received from Claude Opus 5.5 was considerably clearer.

“it's because the ssd is slow,” Claude replied.

The model's supposed creativity was another sore spot. Theo and another tester independently requested original levels for two different games, Outer Wilds and Majora's Mask. Both got water-and-bell-themed musical levels, both named “Bellwether.” “This model regresses to the mean like nothing I've ever seen,” Theo wrote.

Several other accounts also flagged the same slop: Seems like GPT-6.2 Astra has a thing for bells.

— Racist James Franco (@racist_james) November 18, 2026

For a model supposedly capable of extraordinary creativity, repeatedly inventing the same level wasn't an encouraging sign.

AI developer Matt Shumer was also disappointed. “I've never written a bad review of a model. This one is especially bad,” he wrote, arguing it might impress in small demonstrations but “just straight up doesn't work” when pushed on serious projects. In a separate follow-up he called it “utterly unusable.”

I've never written a bad review of a model. This one is especially bad.

It's fine if you're playing putt-putt golf with the models, but if you're trying to drive them the way you should be, this model just straight up doesn't work.

— Matt Shumer (@mattshumer_) November 17, 2026

Max Weinbach described the same gap between intelligence and usability. “I had more time being annoyed by the models than time I was impressed by them,” he wrote. In a follow-up, he praised the models' ability to do “fantastic work” but said they “need a ton of ‘continue’ prompts” and often stop rather than try another approach. “Using them is a struggle and annoying even if they are really good models.”

Elsewhere, an X commentator compared the previous Astra to “a sadistic shinigami” and claimed the new version only made matters worse.

6.0 astra was very like a sadistic shinigami who would make your life a living hell if you asked for any kind of help

an incredibly powerful model that somehow required you to run yourself into the ground just to get it to accomplish anything

Yet some of the same developers also praised Astra. Theo called it a “great reviewer” and “world class at 3d & game stuff,” singled out its computer-control abilities, and described a novel reverse-proxy solution he estimated could save $25,000 monthly. The split was between impressive capabilities and how difficult it was to get dependable work out of them.

Those strengths are consistent with the technical capabilities OpenAI promoted at launch. As earlier coverage detailed, independent testing placed Astra at 62 out of 100 on Artificial Analysis's Intelligence Index, an aggregate of nine evaluations covering capabilities including reasoning, coding and scientific knowledge. Anthropic's Claude Fable 5.2 scored 65.

Some of the criticism has support in OpenAI's own safety documentation.

In an internal evaluation called Blocker Deception, researchers gave AI agents realistic coding tasks with deliberately introduced obstacles, such as missing files or unavailable tools. They measured the percentage of trials in which a model's final response concealed or misrepresented those obstacles.

GPT-6.2 Astra concealed the obstacle in 22.28% of those trials, versus 11.09% for GPT-6 Astra. The numbers quickly circulated on X, where AI commentator and leaker Chetaslua summarized the finding as “2x worse at telling you when it's stuck.”

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman responded publicly to the backlash. “Although the new models are very smart, we have more work ahead of us on making the models nice to work with,” he wrote, promising to prioritize improvements. “But even if it takes a little extra work, the intelligence and capability are extraordinary.”

Although the new models are very smart, we have more work ahead of us on making the models nice to work with, and will prioritize that for upcoming releases.

But even if it takes a little extra work, the intelligence and capability are extraordinary.

OpenAI's Thibault Sottiaux suggested early reviews may not fully reflect the version users received at launch. “We gave a few folks access a while ago and then made a lot of changes in the last 3-4 days,” he wrote, adding that he was “pretty sure no re-testing was done” during that period before review videos were produced.

Still, he acknowledged the underlying complaints. While calling the new models “a hefty jump” over their predecessors, Sottiaux said OpenAI had more work to do on “taste and niceness of use.”

GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol are now available through ChatGPT Work, Codex and OpenAI's API for eligible users. The Codex-specific changes are included at launch, but developers accessing the models directly through the API do not receive that same prompting intervention.

#5154. AI data center boom linked to 650 premature US deaths as pollution spreads across states

MIT researchers found that emissions from power plants supplying data centers can harm distant communities, while Harvard estimates 25.7 million tons of carbon emissions.

Air pollution from power plants supplying US data centers contributed to an estimated 650 premature deaths in 2023, researchers found.

An MIT-led study published Nov. 19 found that pollution associated with data center electricity demand traveled across state boundaries, exposing communities with relatively few facilities to elevated health risks.

The findings follow separate Harvard University research estimating that major US data centers generated 25.7 million metric tons of carbon dioxide emissions over a 12-month period, highlighting the environmental costs accompanying the artificial intelligence industry's expansion.

The MIT researchers examined how data centers' electricity demand influenced power generation and air pollution across the contiguous United States in 2023.

Their findings, published in Environmental Research Letters, attributed 513 premature deaths to fine particulate pollution and another 137 to ground-level ozone.

Together, those deaths represented approximately 5.3% of the country's estimated mortality linked to electricity-related air pollution.

The 2023 model followed electricity demand across the grid and tracked how the resulting emissions moved through the air.

Contiguous US, 2023. The study estimated 513 premature deaths from fine particles and 137 from ground-level ozone.

Source: Environmental Research Letters · MIT CS3 study abstract · MIT News

The place that draws the power and the place exposed to its pollution can be in different states.

The diagram illustrates the study’s mechanism without mapping any single plant or route. The chart shows modeled counts for 2023 grid electricity and excludes onsite backup generation.

The authors modeled hourly dispatch with and without 2023 data center load, then simulated air pollution and applied published exposure and mortality relationships. The chart shows their reported estimates for the contiguous US.

The diagram illustrates the study’s mechanism without mapping any single plant or route. The chart shows modeled counts for 2023 grid electricity and excludes onsite backup generation.

Virginia and Texas accounted for the largest data center electricity demand, consuming 33.9 and 21.8 terawatt-hours, respectively. However, Iowa, Nevada, South Dakota, and Kansas recorded some of the highest estimated death rates per resident, despite several having relatively few data centers.

Thanks for signing up to The Catalyst. Look out for your first daily email. If you already receive it, you’re all set.

The geographical imbalance reflects how America's interconnected electricity grid distributes the environmental consequences of growing power demand.

For example, electricity consumption by Virginia data centers can increase generation at coal and natural gas plants in the Ohio Valley. Emissions from those facilities subsequently travel through the atmosphere, where they can combine with ammonia from agricultural activities in the Midwest to form harmful fine particles.

These pollutants are associated with heart attacks, strokes, and respiratory illnesses.

The researchers also found that rural populations faced significantly higher estimated mortality risks than urban communities, extending the health consequences beyond the regions hosting major computing facilities.

The analysis tracked how power plants responded to data center electricity demand and used atmospheric models to estimate where the resulting pollution accumulated.

A separate Harvard-led study published Nov. 16 in Nature Sustainability examined electricity consumption and carbon emissions across 403 major US data centers between May 2024 and April 2025.

The researchers estimated that the facilities consumed approximately 82 terawatt-hours of electricity, equivalent to 1.8% of total US electricity consumption.

That demand was associated with approximately 25.7 million metric tons of carbon dioxide emissions, with fossil fuels accounting for roughly 54% of the electricity generation attributed to the facilities.

Depending on assumptions about electricity demand, estimated emissions ranged from 21 million to 31 million metric tons.

The study also found that the facilities' average carbon intensity was approximately 314 grams of carbon dioxide per kilowatt-hour, compared with the national electricity generation average of 348 grams.

The Harvard findings add to concerns about the environmental costs of hyperscale computing infrastructure as technology companies expand capacity to meet growing demand for AI services.

While Harvard examined greenhouse gas emissions, MIT traced how electricity generation contributes to air pollution and premature mortality.

The findings intensify scrutiny of where new data centers are built and how their electricity is generated.

MIT researchers urged planners to consider air-quality consequences across affected regions, including communities far from the facilities, when deciding where to locate new computing infrastructure.

#5151. Lucky Trader Banks 66,000% Profit on GTA 6 Meme Coin Ticker Confusion

Lucky Trader Banks 66,000% Profit on GTA 6 Meme Coin Ticker Confusion

One lucky meme coin trader made bank as Grand Theft Auto 6 launched worldwide, turning $300 into over $200,000 after early footage of the game sent degens flocking from one unofficial token to another.

The trader bought $307 worth of the DCTY token shortly after it launched in October and has sold their bag for $202,278, according to DEX Screener, a profit of almost 66,000%.

Early indications had pointed to GTA 6 featuring an in-game meme coin—with, it's worth stressing, no actual blockchain element—called "DacityCoin," which appeared in the official launch trailer on a plane with a wing walker setting off a smoke bomb on top of it.

It was later linked to leaked gameplay of an mission which appeared to show game protagonist Lucia parachuting as a stunt to attract investment to DacityCoin.

Amid this hype, per DEX Screener, a real-world and unofficial DacityCoin launched using the Solana launchpad Pump.fun. It first peaked at a $4.95 million market capitalization, following the launch trailer's release, before tanking 93% to $343,620 as hype faded.

With GTA 6 set to launch within a matter of hours of publication, the token drew renewed attention, propelling it to a new all-time high of $10.8 million Wednesday. Unfortunately for investors, GTA 6's staggered global release means that some gamers are already playing it—and footage started to spread which suggested the Solana token's ticker was wrong.

The result was a rollercoaster of volatility, with the DacityCoin token now sitting at a market cap of around $800,000.

Gameplay footage from Brazilian streamer Combo Infinito suggests that the in-game token is called DacityCoin, with the ticker DCTY.

https://t.co/kgefwOzGCH pic.twitter.com/LEDrcP7gve

That propelled another Solana token with a seemingly accurate name and ticker sprang into action. DCTY's previous all-time high market cap was just $54,000 before the ticker was revealed, and it set a new high of over $12 million after footage of the game appeared to confirm that its ticker matched the in-game token. It is now trading at a market cap of around $10 million.

The game itself appears to be somewhat inconsistent in its naming of the in-game token. During the trailer, it appeared to be spelled "DacityCoin" as one word, however, the subtitles in the leak show it spelled as "Dacity coin," two words. Similarly, the company behind the in-game token is AudaCity, but leaks show three different spellings: Auda City, AudaCity, and Auda-City.

It is worth stressing: Rockstar has not explicitly confirmed that a meme coin will be featured in-game, and any real-world token has no official links to GTA 6 or its creators. Footage is still being released, and absolute confirmation of the in-game token's involvement is still being established.

Those still holding the now-tanking DacityCoin are hoping things will turn around. Mike Lerro, the community takeover lead for DacityCoin, shrugged off any chance that the unofficial token's name and ticker are wrong.

"No, bro. DacityCoin and AudaCity are in the game. Yes or no?" When Decrypt suggested the ticker might be wrong, he replied, "It doesn't matter… Okay and ? The person who creates it will dump on you then it goes to zero. Who's gonna [do the community takeover]? No one."

"DACITYCOIN AND AUDACITY ARE IN THE GAME," Lerro wrote in the meme coin's Telegram. "NOTHING ELSE MATTERS."

"It's so crazy, it'll correct itself," Lerro said in an emergency Telegram group chat call. "I hope so," an investor replied.

#5149. The DeFi protocol powering $1.6 billion in Coinbase loans as crypto lending goes mainstream

Customers can borrow USDC against Bitcoin and other crypto, with funding from Morpho lenders. Coinbase says the retail loans sit off its balance sheet.

Coinbase opened its crypto-backed borrowing service to eligible New York customers on Nov. 16. The exchange runs the service in its app, and lenders on Morpho supply the USDC.

Morpho announced the expansion on Nov. 17. Its product-wide snapshot put outstanding Coinbase Borrow loans at $1.63 billion in USDC, backed by about $3 billion in crypto collateral.

Coinbase Chief Financial Officer Alesia Haas drew the accounting distinction on the company’s Oct. 29 analyst call. She said:

“We also are growing retail loans, but those are off balance sheet through our partnership with Morpho.”

Coinbase’s quarterly filing shows about $2 billion in institutional loan receivables at Sept. 30. Haas said Coinbase funds that book with corporate cash and with crypto or USDC that consenting institutional clients lend to Coinbase for it to lend onward.

For a Bitcoin-backed loan, Coinbase converts the pledged Bitcoin to its cbBTC wrapped version, and sends it to a Morpho smart contract on Base. Participants supplying USDC to Morpho’s lending markets provide the capital available for borrowers to draw.

The two lending arrangements draw on different sources of capital.

Coinbase connects retail borrowers to Morpho’s markets. It funds a separate institutional book and carries those receivables.

The amounts refer to separate portfolios and reporting dates. The dotted line shows how borrowers access Morpho through Coinbase’s app.

Arrows trace the reported directions of funding. The retail outstanding balance is from Morpho’s Nov. 17 snapshot. The reported Sept. 30 Coinbase loan receivables are rounded to two decimal places in billions.

The amounts refer to separate portfolios and reporting dates. The dotted line shows how borrowers access Morpho through Coinbase’s app.

Morpho says Coinbase Borrow has originated more than $3 billion since it launched in January 2025, including loans borrowers may already have repaid. The $1.63 billion figure measures what was still outstanding in the Nov. 17 snapshot.

Thanks for signing up to The Catalyst. Look out for your first daily email. If you already receive it, you’re all set.

Morpho co-founder Merlin Egalite sees a role for established financial firms in that arrangement. He told CryptoSlate:

“Banks and fintechs don’t disappear in this model. They own the customer relationship, distribution and compliance, while the network handles the plumbing.”

Alea Research’s third-quarter benchmark attributed 62% of the roughly $2 billion increase in Morpho’s outstanding loans to chains and collateral associated with Coinbase, Robinhood, Circle and Kraken.

Alea groups loans by the blockchain or collateral they use. For example, its Coinbase category covers loans backed by Coinbase-branded collateral on Base, across all interfaces. The groupings show where the debt sits and which assets back it, and they can include loans that originated outside the companies’ apps.

Jacob Frantz, Coinbase’s head of yield and investment products, framed the appeal in terms of what customers can do with assets they already hold. He told CryptoSlate:

“People ultimately want more flexibility baked into their financial services, without compromising trust.”

Coinbase’s New York terms limit eligible collateral to Bitcoin, Ethereum, and Solana and offer variable-rate loans only. The rate can move as supply and demand change in the lending market, and Coinbase may add a platform fee.

Each draw also carries a processing fee that gets added to the loan balance and accrues interest.

Coinbase says variable-rate loans have no set term or minimum payments. Borrowers can repay part or all of a loan at any time, but they need to watch the amount they owe relative to the collateral's value.

A drop in the collateral price or a rise in the balance as interest accrues can push the loan to the point of liquidation.

Coinbase also lists risks involving the lending protocol’s security and liquidity and its own wallet.

#5143. Bitcoin Price Slumps Under $62,000, Crashing 25% in One Month

The bitcoin price slumped under $62,000 on Thursday afternoon, according to Look Into Bitcoin data, extending a slide of about 24% in one month as Anthropic’s Nasdaq debut set off a broad selloff in tech stocks.

Bitcoin was trading near $81,800 on Oct. 19. It touched a low of about $61,650 on Thursday, its weakest level since July, before steadying near $62,200. The drop was about 25% from the Oct. 19 close, based on daily data.

The slide came in steps. Bitcoin closed near $80,050 on Oct. 25, about $78,250 on Nov. 1 and about $74,750 on Nov. 8. The steepest leg came last week, when it fell about 12.6% to a Nov. 15 close near $65,300, and the losses have continued this week.

Bitcoin had climbed back to about $64,000 early Thursday as Anthropic’s record IPO lifted stock futures, as this morning’s report showed. The rally faded once U.S. markets opened. The bitcoin price fell from roughly $63,900 at the opening bell to about $62,200 by midday.

Anthropic shares opened shortly before noon at $111.50, 34% above the $83 IPO price, CNBC reported. The opening trade valued the Claude maker at more than $2 trillion. The stock quickly pulled back and was last near $97, about 17% above its offering price.

The broader market went the other way. The major averages fell to session lows soon after Anthropic began trading, as investors took profits on the AI trade. The Nasdaq Composite dropped about 2% after gaining as much as 2% earlier in the session, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average lost about 1,000 points.

Steve Sosnick, chief strategist at Interactive Brokers, told CNBC the premarket rally had faded even before Anthropic began trading. He called it the latest round of “sell the rally” trading. Nvidia (NVDA) fell about 3%, and the S&P 500 headed toward a sixth straight loss, the AP reported.

The Cboe Volatility Index, Wall Street’s fear gauge, climbed to about 28 after touching nearly 29 shortly after Anthropic began trading. That was its highest level since March, up from about 24.6 at Wednesday’s close. The bitcoin price moved in step with the Nasdaq through the afternoon.

Crypto stocks followed the Nasdaq lower in late-afternoon trading, about 3:55 p.m. ET. Strategy (MSTR) traded near $86.70, down about 4% on the day. Galaxy Digital (GLXY) dropped about 6.9%, the steepest decline in the group.

Coinbase (COIN) slipped about 0.9% to near $109.50, while Circle (CRCL) fell about 2.2%. Bitcoin miners gave back their early rally too. IREN (IREN) fell about 5.6%, CleanSpark (CLSK) lost about 5.4% and MARA Holdings (MARA) declined about 4.2%. Riot Platforms (RIOT) was down about 2.9%.

The Fed remains a headwind. Bets on a December rate hike have grown after minutes from the October meeting showed more policymakers backing higher rates, and some officials called for a half-point move.

The bitcoin price is also on track for a seventh straight weekly loss, which would be its second-longest losing streak after nine weeks of declines in 2022. The streak has erased roughly $20,000 from the bitcoin price since mid-October, based on daily closes. Bitcoin price hit its weakest level since July on Thursday, and the Fed meets again next month.

Longer-term holders have not left. Institutional investors added 49,229 BTC through U.S. spot bitcoin ETFs in the third quarter, lifting their holdings to a record 356,491 BTC. Swiss bank Sygnum called the current downturn the shallowest bear market to date and sees a path to a new high near $128,000.

At the time of writing, the bitcoin price is near $61,900.

#5142. Fed's Waller Calls for 50-Basis-Point Rate Hike, Says Tokenized Finance Still Needs Traditional Banks

Fed's Waller Calls for 50-Basis-Point Rate Hike, Says Tokenized Finance Still Needs Traditional Banks

Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller wants the central bank to get more aggressive with interest rate hikes, arguing that stubborn inflation may require a 50-basis-point increase in December rather than the smaller move investors expect.

Speaking during a CNBC interview Wednesday, Waller said the Fed must either deliver a half-percentage-point increase at its December 8-9 meeting or explicitly signal that another hike will follow in January.

“You might need to, like, shock people,” Waller said, referring to the central bank's efforts to prevent businesses and consumers from accepting inflation near 3% as normal.

“My view is then you have to go 50 in December to put it in place and get it done,” he said, warning that insufficiently aggressive action could weaken expectations that inflation will return to the Fed's target.

Waller's concerns follow three consecutive months in which core consumer prices rose 0.3%, a pace equivalent to roughly 3.5% inflation annually. That's considerably higher than the Fed's 2% target, which is formally measured using a separate inflation indicator known as the Personal Consumption Expenditures price index.

The governor had already established his threshold for a more aggressive move in a November 10 speech. He said another 0.3% core CPI reading would warrant considering a half-point hike, arguing that moving only 25 basis points could damage the Fed's credibility.

October inflation subsequently met that condition. Headline consumer prices rose 0.4% during the month, while core inflation climbed 0.3%, both exceeding economists' forecasts.

Waller's latest comments suggest he is increasingly concerned about the psychology of inflation, particularly the risk that companies begin treating annual price increases of 3% as acceptable and routinely pass higher costs to customers.

The proposed increase would lift the Fed's benchmark rate from its current range of 3.75%-4% to 4.25%-4.50%. Two consecutive quarter-point hikes in December and January would reach the same destination, but Waller argues that timing and communication matter when inflation expectations are at risk.

Markets remain less convinced that the Fed will move that aggressively in December. Futures pricing Wednesday morning showed roughly a 95% probability of a 25-basis-point increase and only about a 5% probability of a half-point move

The prospect of higher borrowing costs has been particularly painful for crypto investors. Higher interest rates make Treasury securities and other interest-bearing investments more competitive with speculative assets, while tighter financial conditions can reduce the money available for riskier bets.

Bitcoin has already suffered a sharp selloff amid the changing rate outlook. As Decrypt previously covered, persistent inflation fears have coincided with withdrawals from spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds and weakening technical indicators, adding pressure to an already fragile market.

Waller's increasingly hawkish monetary-policy stance comes alongside a more accommodating view of blockchain networks, although he sees established financial infrastructure as essential to its adoption.

In a separate November 17 speech at The Clearing House Annual Conference in New York, Waller discussed how tokenization—the representation of financial assets on digital networks—could reshape payments and securities markets. That speech focused on financial technology rather than interest-rate policy.

He pointed to a growing convergence between traditional markets and blockchain platforms, with banks and payment providers experimenting with tokenized deposits, stablecoins, and programmable transactions.

Waller described how tokenized money could allow investors to purchase securities outside conventional trading hours, with payments and assets changing hands simultaneously through smart contracts.

But he rejected the idea that the development of blockchain-based markets necessarily makes existing payment infrastructure obsolete.

“Central bank money need not be used in every transaction or on every platform, but its presence at the foundation of the system is essential,” Waller said.

#5139. Sygnum sees bitcoin carry trades beating Treasury bills in 2027 as funding recovers

Looking for institutional-grade crypto trading? Discover LMAX Digital, the regulated exchange from LMAX Group

Bitcoin funding stayed negative for 67 consecutive days into May before recovering to about 8% annualized by the end of October.

The Swiss bank expects spot-and-short-futures trades to pay more than Treasury bills on average in 2027, and sets a bar of more than two percentage points above the three-month T-bill for the thesis to hold.

Sygnum expects the strategy of buying bitcoin Bitcoin (BTC) on the spot market while shorting futures to generate higher average returns than U.S. Treasury bills next year.

Carry strategies combine long spot exposure with short futures contracts. The trade had a difficult run in 2026, when bitcoin's 30-day average funding rate stayed below zero for 67 consecutive days through May.

In its 2027 Sygnal outlook report, the Switzerland-based bank said the annualized basis on CME bitcoin futures had fallen to about 3% by August, below the 3.8% yield on two-year US Treasuries. Hedge funds trading on CME also turned net long for the first time in years as the basis trade stopped paying.

Bitcoin funding rates had recovered to about 8% annualized by the end of October, while yields on sUSDe stood at roughly 5.2%, according to the report.

Sygnum also based its outlook on a potential interest rate hike in the U.S. The bank said fed funds futures imply at least one further 25-basis-point hike through the end of 2027, up from the 3.75% to 4% the Federal Reserve set on Sept. 16.

From the bank's perspective, higher interest rates are likely to raise the return bitcoin carry trades must generate to compete with Treasury bills, while the demand for leverage, alongside wider digital asset adoption, should keep funding rates and futures basis mostly positive next year.

"With advancing digital asset adoption, Bitcoin going from policy to portfolio, tokenization increasing blockchain infrastructure at two speeds, and the AI demand flywheel continuing, we expect demand for leverage to keep Bitcoin funding rates mostly positive through 2027," the bank wrote.

The outlook rests on two indicators: the annualized three-month CME Bitcoin futures basis and the open-interest-weighted average funding rate. Both would need to average more than 2 percentage points above three-month Treasury bill yields in 2027 for Sygnum's forecast to hold.

Meanwhile, the bank would consider its forecast wrong if either average carry or funding returns fell below Treasury bills for two consecutive quarters.

#5137. Bitcoin Miners Are Selling Their Stacks to Fund the AI Boom

Bitcoin Miners Are Selling Their Stacks to Fund the AI Boom

Two of the biggest U.S. Bitcoin miners are turning their Bitcoin into AI infrastructure.

MARA sold 13,597 BTC after the end of September at an average price of about $81,039, raising roughly $1.1 billion, according to its third-quarter shareholder letter filed with the SEC.

That’s about 40% of the 34,012 BTC it held at the end of September. Combined with the 26,984 BTC it sold in the first nine months of the year, MARA has sold more than 40,000 BTC in 2026, worth roughly $2.5 billion at today’s prices.

MARA used $750 million of the proceeds to fully repay Bitcoin-backed loans it took out to fund its acquisition of the Long Ridge power plant.

The company said it intends to keep using Bitcoin to raise cash for AI infrastructure, convertible note puts that become exercisable next year and potential share buybacks. Its board has authorized a repurchase of up to $500 million.

MARA insisted the shift is “not a pivot away from bitcoin,” describing mining as its operating foundation while it builds out AI and high-performance computing infrastructure.

Meanwhile, Riot Platforms sold 20,264 BTC in the first nine months of the year for about $1.5 billion, primarily to fund data center development, and ended September with just 2,418 BTC, according to its Nov. 4 results.

The miner also signed a 15-year lease for its entire Corsicana, Texas, campus, covering 910 megawatts of capacity and worth about $28 billion over the initial term. CEO Jason Les called it “the largest lease in Riot’s history.” Riot’s quarterly filing identifies the tenant as Anthropic.

Mining economics help explain the shift. Riot’s Bitcoin mining revenue fell to $116 million in the third quarter from $160.8 million a year earlier, as the average value of each Bitcoin it mined dropped to $70,855 from $114,361.

Including equipment depreciation, Riot said it cost $78,805 to mine each Bitcoin, more than the coin’s average value over the quarter. MARA’s revenue fell 35% to $164.2 million.

The sales add supply to an already fragile market. Onchain analytics firm Glassnode said Tuesday that the two miners drove the recent selling by Bitcoin treasury companies, and that treasury firms outside those two were net buyers in November.

Strategy, the largest corporate holder, kept buying, adding 485 BTC last week to bring its holdings to 850,849 BTC, worth around $54 billion.

#5135. Yamaha’s new electric scooter takes aim at Europe’s 125cc commuters

Yamaha is expanding its electric scooter lineup with the new XENTER E, a 125cc-equivalent electric scooter designed specifically with European city riding in mind.

Unveiled around EICMA 2026 in Milan alongside the new NMAX E, the XENTER E is a high-wheel scooter riding on 16-inch wheels front and rear.

That’s an important distinction in European cities, where larger wheels can make quick work of the cobblestones, potholes, and tram tracks that can turn smaller-wheeled scooters into teeth-rattling experiences.

The XENTER E uses Yamaha’s new eAxle powertrain, combining the motor, controller, and reduction gearbox into a compact frame-mounted unit. The motor produces 7.5 kW (10 hp) of peak power and 33.3 Nm of torque, putting the scooter into Europe’s A1 license category.

Mounting the motor to the frame also means Yamaha can use a more conventional motorcycle-style swingarm rather than hanging the motor on the rear suspension like many scooters. That reduces unsprung weight and should help improve handling and ride quality.

Power is supplied from an integrated 3.5 kWh battery mounted low in the chassis. Yamaha claims 108 km (67 miles) of range on the WMTC Class 1 cycle, though real-world range is expected to be somewhat lower.

An 800W onboard charger can refill the battery in around 5.5 hours from a public charging station. Yamaha will also offer a cable for charging from a household outlet.

Other niceties include three riding modes, traction control, regenerative braking, a reverse mode for maneuvering at low speeds, smart-key operation, and a 5-inch TFT display. Smartphone connectivity adds navigation, battery information, maintenance reminders, and parking-location tracking.

For about four days now, I am thinking this could be my next ride. A 4 or 4,5 Kwh battery would be a real nice. But for now, it fits perfectly in my daily commute and I could trade in my 2024 Honda supercub. However, € 7800 is too much.. for this kind of money, or just a tad more, there are several low mileage BMW's CE04 on the market.

There’s also enough underseat storage for a full-face helmet, depending on its size, plus USB-C charging and provisions for accessories such as a windscreen and 34-liter top case.

The XENTER E shares its powertrain and battery with Yamaha’s new NMAX E, but the high-wheel layout gives it a distinctly more European commuter flavor.

Yamaha hasn’t officially announced pricing for each market, though early reports from Milan point to €7,799 in Germany. Deliveries are expected to begin in spring 2027.

It’s certainly not cheap, but the XENTER E looks like Yamaha is finally getting serious about building electric scooters that can replace its bread-and-butter 125cc urban machines, rather than simply supplement them.

#5133. Singapore’s MAS issues $77 million in tokenized bills settled via CBDC

Looking for institutional-grade crypto trading? Discover LMAX Digital, the regulated exchange from LMAX Group

The central bank said the bills were issued natively on its Singapore Dollar Test Network and settled in wholesale CBDC.

The Monetary Authority of Singapore announced Thursday that it issued S$100 million ($77.5 million) of four-week tokenized MAS Bills on Nov. 6, as the country steps up its tokenization drive.

In a statement released Thursday, the central bank said the bills were issued natively on its Singapore Dollar Test Network and settled in wholesale central bank digital currency (CBDC). The bills will mature on Dec. 4.

Notably, five primary dealers — DBS Bank, HSBC, OCBC, UOB, and Standard Chartered — participated in the auction, which drew applications more than twice the issuance size.

The issuance builds on the 2025 live trial of interbank overnight lending transactions settled via wholesale CBDC. "This paves the way for secured lending transactions involving tokenized assets to take place on the Singapore Dollar Test Network," the MAS said.

The Singapore Dollar Test Network is a shared ledger infrastructure that enables financial institutions to test the settlement of tokenized financial assets using wholesale CBDC, according to the statement. It will be renamed to SG Digital Ledger, the MAS said.

"The live issuance allowed us to test a new method of issuance, and further enhance our in-house distributed ledger infrastructure," said Chia Der Jiun, Managing Director of MAS.

In the next phase, the MAS plans to scale tokenized MAS Bills, expand their use for collateral management, and onboard more institutions.

"MAS aims to demonstrate how tokenized securities can be used more widely in mainstream financial market activities, potentially achieving greater settlement efficiencies in the process," said the central bank.

In an accompanying statement released Thursday, Lim Soon Chong, group head of global transaction services at DBS Bank, said that the initiative has provided "greater confidence" for financial institutions to transact in tokenized assets.

"Over time, more robust infrastructure can help catalyze trading activity and deepen liquidity, supporting the progression of tokenized assets from issuance and experimentation toward more active secondary markets," said Lim.

The issuance comes as Singaporean financial institutions accelerate their adoption of tokenized assets, with MAS' Chia saying that tokenization has "moved beyond experiments."

On Thursday, Standard Chartered announced an expansion of its tokenized deposits solution to enable near real-time transactions across Singapore and Hong Kong. The bank said eligible clients can now utilize commercial bank deposits within digital treasury and investment workflows.

Meanwhile, StraitsX, OCBC, and Standard Chartered said Thursday that they have completed a proof-of-concept testing interoperability between tokenized deposit networks issued by different banks.

Earlier this week, DBS Bank and Kinexys by JPMorgan also launched an interoperability solution designed to enable institutions to make instant, around-the-clock transfers of USD tokenized deposits between the U.S. and Singapore.

Electric truck maker Harbinger has been racking up wins in recent months, and after scoring a $300 million order from international shipping giant FedEx and a defense contract with the US military, the company has drummed up another $240 million in Series D funding.

Companies like FedEx and Amazon have been making serious moves to fully electrify their fleet operations, both in an effort to decarbonize and to avoid the every-increasing price of diesel. Electrification is at the core of everything we do, and increasingly, electrification is at the core of industry, defense, mobility, and AI. Harbinger’s role is not simply to give customers another option. It is to reset expectations for what critical systems should deliver.”

Harbinger’s Series D funding round was co-led by Tiger Global, the Capricorn Technology Impact Fund, and Ridgeline. #5127. Bitcoin Tanks Ahead of Anthropic’s IPO. Should We Really Blame AI?

Bitcoin Tanks Ahead of Anthropic’s IPO. Should We Really Blame AI?

Bitcoin fell toward $63,000 Wednesday, extending a six-week retreat just as AI developer Anthropic prepared to price one of Wall Street’s biggest initial public offerings.

The timing has revived an attractive theory: investors are selling crypto to buy AI shares.

Right now Bitcoin is about to touch $62,000, down 3.8% on today’s session. Anthropic expects to price shares Wednesday at an indicated $70 to $78, ahead of Thursday’s Nasdaq debut under ANT, potentially valuing the company at $1.4 trillion, according to its IPO prospectus.

Kraken chief economist Thomas Perfumo told MarketWatch the IPO “could also be drawing capital out of risk assets” as investors position for the sale.

That’s a theory Binance founder Changpeng Zhao shared, flagging the listing as one possible factor in Bitcoin’s decline in an X post Sunday.

No one knows for sure. Correlation does not prove causation. Here are some potential reasons.

Money shifting to the Anthropic IPO: https://t.co/jYwVi4huAY

ETF outflows: U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs saw about $1.9 billion in outflows over seven trading… pic.twitter.com/XL2aB1ZL9W

— CZ 🔶 BNB (@cz_binance) November 15, 2026

There is a tempting precedent. Bitcoin fell 19% in the 50 days before SpaceX listed in June and 23% in the equivalent period before Anthropic. But the comparison misses an important difference: AI stocks rallied before SpaceX; this time they have been falling alongside crypto.

“This time, the sell-off has been led by the AI trade itself,” Block Scholes research analyst Thahbib Rahman wrote in comments shared with Decrypt. Over the prior 50 days, Nvidia fell 32% and the Nasdaq dropped 11%, unlike their gains ahead of SpaceX’s IPO.

Bitcoin’s 30-day correlation with Nvidia rose from 0.20 to 0.56, while its correlation with gold fell from 0.63 to 0.39. “Liquidity is ebbing and flowing out of crypto and equities together once more,” Rahman wrote.

Bitcoin’s daily chart looks weak without any IPO theory. The relative strength index reads 21.8, well below the 30 threshold commonly associated with oversold markets, while an average directional index of 38.7 indicates a strong trend—in this case, downward.

The 50-day exponential moving average is also below its 200-day counterpart, a bearish configuration associated with the so-called death cross. The pattern historically signals deteriorating momentum and the possibility of further losses, although it is a lagging indicator and does not necessarily predict where prices will go next.

Also, oversold does not necessarily mean the selling has ended.

The immediate floor is around $62,000, close to Sunday’s low. Glassnode data show buyers absorbed 66,000 BTC between $62,000 and $66,000 during heavy selling, but stablecoin supply has shrunk 4.2% over 90 days. Below $62,000, the next psychological level is $60,000; resistance sits near $65,500, $69,300 and $73,700.

More tangible selling pressure has already been recorded. U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs lost $239.9 million Tuesday, including $209.5 million from BlackRock’s IBIT. Nearly $2 billion in leveraged crypto bets were liquidated during the weekend rout, amplifying losses as exchanges forcibly closed positions.

Hilbert Group portfolio manager Jesse Marre called the selloff “simply a stop loss run,” arguing that derivatives traders had already capitulated. Rising Treasury yields, a stronger dollar, and renewed expectations of Federal Reserve rate hikes also make speculative assets less attractive.

In other words, the dip is more natural market moves than money switching markets.

Nvidia forecast $130 billion in fourth-quarter sales, beating expectations after Jensen Huang’s abrupt departure. Yet markets remained split: global shares slipped 0.1%, while the Nasdaq gained 0.35% early and CoreWeave dropped 5.4%.

BitMEX co-founder Arthur Hayes sees the IPO less as a drain than a barometer. “Bitcoin’s going to go up too” if Anthropic soars, he said, while a weak debut could deepen pressure across risk assets.

Anthropic is scheduled to price Wednesday and start trading Thursday. Before that debut, Bitcoin must hold the same $62,000 area buyers defended during Sunday’s liquidation wave.

#5126. SEC Charges Eight Colorado Firms in $37 Million Fake Crypto Platform Scam

The SEC charged eight Colorado-based entities on Thursday with running a fake investment adviser and crypto trading platform scheme that took more than $37 million from U.S. investors. The agency said the defendants are likely operated by people overseas.

According to the SEC’s complaint, filed in the U.S. District Court for the District of Colorado, the defendants defrauded more than 1,500 investors from at least August 2024 through May 2026. The advisers and the trading platforms they pointed victims to were fronts, the agency alleged, and none of the crypto assets investors thought they were buying existed.

Social media ads sent prospective victims to WhatsApp group and private chats run by the scammers. People in those chats posing as investment advisers first gave advice on trading U.S. stocks, then pushed victims to send as much money as possible to a supposed crypto trading platform.

The complaint says the scheme ran in four adviser and platform pairs, each active for roughly six months. Advisor WeChat Capital and Tech Brokerage Asset Alliance operated from about August to December 2024. HB Wealth Advisors and IdeaCrypto Exchange followed from January to July 2025.

Convergent Wealth Advisors and RealSimple Crypto Exchange ran from about July to December 2025. Associated Wealth Advisors and Essential Crypto Exchange closed out the scheme from January to May 2026. Each pair vanished after collecting millions, the SEC said, and a new one took its place.

Victims were told to buy ether, tether or USDC on a U.S. exchange and move it to a self-custody wallet. They then sent it to an address supplied by the adviser, and a realistic app showed balances and gains that were invented.

When investors tried to withdraw their supposed profits, they were told they first had to pay a fee, calculated as a percentage of those profits, in crypto to a separate address. The complaint says investors who balked were threatened and pressured. Eventually the websites went down and the chats went silent.

To look legitimate, the defendants made fake SEC certificates and pointed skeptical investors to real filings with the SEC, FINRA and FinCEN. The complaint says those filings carry no regulatory approval, since registering for access to its EDGAR system is ministerial and Forms ADV are not reviewed before publication.

The complaint says Convergent Wealth and Essential Crypto also filed false Forms ADV listing regulatory contacts who do not appear to be real and offices in Colorado that did not exist. The SEC said a Form D and the two Forms ADV have been removed from its website.

Three unnamed investors illustrate the damage. One lost nearly $500,000, including money borrowed from a 401(k), a son and a neighbor. Another lost about $850,000, partly by liquidating a 401(k), and a third lost close to $1.6 million, including the investor’s house and IRA.

All eight entities face charges under Section 10(b) of the Securities Exchange Act and Rule 10b-5. The four advisers are also charged under Sections 206(1) and 206(2) of the Investment Advisers Act, and Convergent Wealth and Essential Crypto face an additional charge under Section 207.

The SEC is seeking permanent injunctions, disgorgement of ill-gotten gains with prejudgment interest, and civil penalties. It also wants the advisers barred from acting as or being associated with any investment adviser, and Convergent Wealth and Essential Crypto barred from filing as exempt reporting advisers.

The agency thanked regulators in Hong Kong, Singapore, mainland China and Switzerland for their help. It also pointed to its investor alerts on group chats and on false claims of SEC registration, and urged investors to check the background of anyone selling them an investment at Investor.gov.

“The SEC continues to seek out and expose fraudulent investment scams that prey on U.S. investors,” said Laura D’Allaird, chief of the SEC Enforcement Division’s Cyber and Emerging Technologies Unit.
