#4998. MoonPay seeks US bank charter for stablecoin, custody services

MoonPay’s proposed national trust bank would offer stablecoin issuance and redemption, reserve management and digital asset custody under federal oversight.

Crypto payments firm MoonPay has applied for a US national trust bank charter to offer stablecoin issuance and redemption, reserve management and digital asset custody services.

According to an OCC filing, MoonPay submitted its application on Tuesday to establish MoonPay National Trust Bank, a non-depository institution headquartered in Miami Beach, Florida. The proposed bank would not accept traditional deposits or issue loans.

MoonPay already provides stablecoin issuance infrastructure to businesses, including support for branded digital dollars. If approved, the charter would allow its proposed banking subsidiary to provide stablecoin and custody services under federal supervision.

The application comes as US regulators prepare to implement the GENIUS Act, which takes effect on Jan. 18, 2027, and establishes federal standards for stablecoin issuers, including reserve backing and redemption requirements.

With the filing, MoonPay joins several crypto and payments companies seeking federal trust bank charters, including Rain, Modern Treasury and Block. Coinbase’s charter took effect earlier this month, while Circle received final OCC approval in July.

The rise in crypto firms applying for federal trust bank charters has drawn opposition from community banks. In October, the Independent Community Bankers of America sued the OCC, arguing that the regulator exceeded its authority by allowing non-depository trust banks to conduct activities traditionally associated with commercial banks.

#4997. Meet SHRINCS: Bitcoin's Emerging Frontrunner for a Post-Quantum Signature

Meet SHRINCS: Bitcoin's Emerging Frontrunner for a Post-Quantum Signature

Blockstream Research Director Jonas Nick, with Mikhail Kudinov and collaborators, published a security analysis on Thursday for SHRINCS, advancing an emerging frontrunner for a post-quantum signature scheme in Bitcoin.

“We need all the possible feedback—engineers, cryptographers, protocol developers,” Kudinov, a post-quantum cryptography researcher at Blockstream, said in reference to a draft of SHRINCS’ Bitcoin Improvement Proposal (BIP). “There are a lot of things to check, test, complain about, or praise."

Notably, SHRINCS is a hash-based signature scheme that leverages SHA-256 to anchor its security in battle-tested primitives that are already used by Bitcoin, representing a conservative effort to minimize the proposal’s trust assumptions.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short Bitcoin with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

That said, the scheme comes with trade-offs, most notably by introducing potential security vulnerabilities at the implementation level if misused. The scheme combines two spending paths: a small, more efficient stateful signature option and a larger, more costly stateless path with fewer security risks on the implementation side.

Although stateful signatures are compact, preserving Bitcoin’s ability to process transactions efficiently, a user can trigger a critical failure—where an attacker can forge a signature for that address and steal funds if a one-time state is accidentally reused. Because SHRINCS’ stateful path relies on one-time keys that can only safely sign a single transaction, wallet developers must carefully track each key’s state.

“It needs to be impossible for the user to behave in a way that this catastrophic event happens,” Nick told Head of MARA Foundation Isabel Foxen Duke during a recent appearance on MARA Foundation TV. “Wallet developers need to deal with this stateful component correctly.”

According to Nick, for SHRINCS to work safely in the real world, its specification and corresponding wallet implementations must automatically enforce the stateless path fallback in any situation where a state counter could possibly be compromised.

While some users might gravitate toward stateless signatures out of caution, Nick warns that widespread adoption could bloat the blockchain and drive up fees across the network.

Bitcoin’s current ECDSA signatures are typically 71 bytes long (and Taproot Schnorr signatures are 64 bytes). Under SHRINCS, stateful signatures are anywhere from 548 to 4,619 bytes, while stateless ones are 5,777 bytes. That said, optimizations of both signature paths have been accelerating with the support of AI-based research, Nick noted.

“We don’t know what the fee market will look like once we have these very big signatures,” he said. “And it’s not just the fee market, it’s also just fewer transactions fit into a block, meaning fewer people can use Bitcoin. And I think this changes the value proposition of Bitcoin.”

As the SHRINCS working group—which includes researchers backed by nonprofits including Brink and OpenSats—continues to refine the proposal’s specification, Blockstream researchers stress that getting the cryptographic foundation right is only half the battle.

Whether the broader Bitcoin ecosystem is ready to embrace SHRINCS’ inherent trade-offs will depend heavily on feedback from the network’s stakeholders in the months ahead. Meanwhile, Nick and Kudinov are requesting review of the proposal and the security analysis.

André Beganski is a Senior Content Manager at MARA Foundation, producing content on topics including the intersection of quantum computing and cryptography. He has previously worked for Decrypt.

#4996. After Launching McGee & Co., Shea McGee Shares 8 Lessons for Opening a Store

My husband Syd and I are both lovers of retail, and have always known one day we’d have a McGee & Co. shop of our own. Over the years, we’ve spent a lot of time jotting down ideas for our own store. Our new flagship is a repository for all that knowledge that we’ve been squirreling away—but it also taught us a few lessons of its own.

Speaking to you now, on the other side of its debut, there are some things we only learned through actually doing. From the importance of developing a training manual to the do-or-die value of a soft launch, here are eight hard-won learnings from our McGee & Co. store launch.

It was important to us that the shop feel like the homes we create for our clients—layered and collected, with a variety of patterns and objects for your eye to explore. Despite the fact that the dollars-per-square-foot model is the traditional method of conceiving an in-store assortment, it was more important for us to remain true to ourselves with this first location: we’re a designer-led brand, not a merchant-led one.

“I’m getting to see our products through new eyes—and I was the one that concepted them!” says Shea. “When you see them in a store setting, pieces can have a lot more detail than you can see online.”

We started by coming up with the sections we envisioned, like a kids’ area, a kitchen zone, and so on. Then we created planograms to see how much we could actually fit, and reconciled with our merchandising team to see what made business sense. Sometimes, that meant pivoting from the early vision. A lighting gallery we had planned, for instance, ended up shifting: We loved the idea, but when we looked at the percentage of lighting to the rest of our sales, we could see clearly that it was a smarter business decision to use this space to showcase more furniture. Instead of the sprawling lighting gallery we had imagined, we created a moody lounge area that can flex to showcase different pieces.

We don’t think small: Our aspirations are to grow nationwide. But however much we scale, it’s critical that we not lose the warm, personal feeling that comes from a standalone store. As McGee & Co. grows its brick-and-mortar operation, that’s one of my biggest goals. And there’s another layer here, too: Being a personality-led business, the team members in our store aren’t just representing our brand—they’re representing me, for better or worse. The design world can sometimes feel closed-off and unapproachable, and it’s always been the McGee mantra—in our content, in our personality on social media, in how we work with clients—to be warm and accessible. Now that attitude needs to trickle down to our store associates, too.

Before we opened, I spent months developing a comprehensive training guide for our associates. It’s essentially Design 101, McGee-style, covering everything from how many inches I place a rug away from a wall, to how to pair and arrange accent tables, to how to layer bedding. We cover every level of the decorating process. Thank goodness for AI—it’s been a lifesaver: I’ll narrate as we go on our walk-throughs, and use those notes as the basis for the training manual. And it’s not a one-and-done deal. We’ll continue to add to this document as we evolve and grow.

Every issue, every era. Explore 100+ years of the Architectural Digest Archive, an unparalleled digital resource for research and inspiration. Start Searching

Having that Design 101 established is a first step, but how do you ensure that the team is really internalizing the lessons? For us, the answer was checkpoints. As our design associates go through training and familiarize themselves with our ways of doing things, we hold check-ins with them to make sure that they’re absorbing our ways of operating. It’s the exact same as we do for the junior interior designers at Studio McGee: The checkpoints allow us to build up mutual confidence, with the aim for them to eventually fly on their own.

Shea plans to have the studio’s senior-level designers hosting regular check-ins with the shop’s design associates.

Personally dropping in myself can serve as another kind of checkpoint, too. With the flagship local, I’m able to stop by regularly in these early days to make sure that our standards are upheld, that our visuals are tight, and the operation is humming. That won’t work for us in every location, but it’s certainly a perk of opening up in our own hometown.

As much as I love a good plan, there’s nothing like real-time feedback to show you what’s working and what’s not. Which is why we kicked off our flagship back in September with a whisper and not a bang. We did a very soft launch with no announcement, no social post. We just opened the doors. As folks wandered in, we learned, and we tweaked. And two weeks later, we opened officially. That soft-launch period was vital for us in getting the kinks out.

One benefit of having had an ecommerce business for so long is that we have rich data on exactly where our customers are. That means that from day one, we already know where we need to open next. While launching in Salt Lake City was a logical place for our flagship, we’re already thinking ahead to how we’ll expand to some of our other biggest markets, like Texas and California.

Located in Salt Lake City’s Trolley Square, the “shop,” as Shea calls it, is 7,500 square feet.

We want to capitalize on the fact that the retail-ecommerce loop is an advantageous cycle: Where you have a retail store, your ecommerce sales lift. People who are aware of your product can go see it in person, give it a sit test, think about it, and then finish the sale online. In store, we can educate them, give them styling suggestions, and show off the quality of the product in ways we can’t online. Even for us, we’re discovering new things about our assortment by merchandising it in the store—we’re seeing it with fresh eyes, and we know our customers will too.

Aside from the obvious metric of profitability, to me, success in these early days means nailing down our systems and processes. It’s not the most glamorous side of this business, but it’s a must. I want to be able to say that we know what it takes to run a store and to make the shopper experience in it as smooth as possible. For instance, I want customers to know how to get to our free design services, and to have a great experience using them. If we can do that, we know we’re on our way to some of our loftier goals, too.

I’m not under any illusions here: This first store is a baptism by fire. Not only are we opening a flagship and planting seeds for our future locations—we’re also doing it in Q4, right before the holidays. But my hope is that at the end of it, we can catch our breath and take a moment to reflect on what worked, what didn’t, and then get to work fixing it. In this business, honesty with yourself is the only way up.

“The kitchen is a working kitchen,” says Shea, who envisions cooking demos and community events enlivening the space.

#4995. Honda shows off its next electric motorcycle, and it’s wilder than you thought

Honda has been getting increasingly serious about electric motorcycles, but if you want to see just how weird the company thinks the future could get, take a look at the Honda EV Outlier Concept.

I got a chance to see the wild-looking machine in person at EICMA in Milan, where it looked like almost nothing else on the show floor. And that’s exactly the point.

The EV Outlier Concept originally debuted at last year’s Japan Mobility Show as Honda’s attempt to imagine an electric motorcycle that isn’t simply a conventional motorcycle with the engine swapped for a battery and motor. In fact, Honda describes the concept as looking toward the future of electric motorcycles beyond 2030.

Instead of a centrally mounted motor driving the rear wheel, the EV Outlier uses motors inside both wheels, giving it all-wheel drive and allowing Honda’s designers to completely rethink the rest of the motorcycle’s layout. The battery is housed in that large central black body, while the rider sits extremely low and behind it.

Honda describes the design philosophy with three words: “Gliding, Ecstasy, and Low.” The first refers to the smooth, nearly silent feeling of electric propulsion, while the second describes the instant acceleration and massive torque available from independently controlled front and rear motors. “Low” is more literal: Honda deliberately dropped the rider’s seating and eye position to create an entirely different sensation from a conventional motorcycle.

There’s even a bucket-style backrest designed to support the rider under hard acceleration and let the rider pivot through corners around their hips.

Cool and fun for Honda engineers to play with, but it seems a big no for reality, or at least a different road reality then mine.

Emergency tight swerves for accident avoidance? Nope, gone. Seeing even less of the road, even without a car in front of you, due to being so low? Not good for me nor the deer I don't avoid due to seeing it too late.

Unsprung mass due to hub motors - lots of literature on that topic, so I'll leave that alone.

Up front, traditional mirrors are replaced by cameras, while a wide digital cockpit can display things like lean angle, riding modes, front motor torque adjustment, and what the two wheels are doing in real time.

Will Honda actually build this thing? Almost certainly not exactly as you see it here. That’s what concepts are for.

But the EV Outlier is still interesting as a statement of intent. Honda is obviously still playing around with the freedom that electric drivetrains offer, and the company is asking what motorcycles could become once designers no longer have to work around engines, fuel tanks, transmissions, and traditional drivetrains.

And judging by what I saw at EICMA, Honda’s answer could get pretty wild.

#4994. Nvidia, AMD, Micron Sink as Anthropic Closes 17% Above IPO Price

Nvidia, AMD, Micron Sink as Anthropic Closes 17% Above IPO Price

Anthropic made stock market history Thursday, raising $81.34 billion in the largest initial IPO share sale ever. But Wall Street's response was considerably less enthusiastic than the demand for the Claude developer's shares.

The stock opened at $111.50 on Nasdaq under the ticker ANT, a 34% premium over its $83 offering price, briefly pushing the company's fully diluted valuation past $2 trillion.

The rally faded quickly, however, with shares dropping toward $93 before closing today at $97.17.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short Anthropic with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

The offering involved 980 million shares and surpassed SpaceX's original $75 billion IPO in June. As Decrypt previously reported, SpaceX's expanded final offering reached $86.25 billion, meaning Anthropic has not surpassed that completed deal.

Investors initially welcomed the listing, sending technology stocks higher before the opening bell. By the afternoon, however, the Nasdaq Composite was down 2.06%, the S&P 500 had fallen 1.9%, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average was off 2.17%.

The selloff extended across the AI supply chain. A Thursday afternoon market heatmap showed Nvidia falling 3.4%, Broadcom losing 2.07%, and memory chipmaker Micron slipping 2.17%. Microsoft was down 1.97%, while cloud infrastructure and software provider Oracle declined 2.97%.

AMD was among the hardest hit, down 7.73% in the day, although its decline had a separate catalyst. Reuters reported that the chipmaker came under pressure after investigative outlet Hunterbrook disclosed that its affiliated investment fund had taken a short position in the company.

The picture was not uniformly negative. Palo Alto Networks rose 6%, CrowdStrike gained 2.24%, and Intel added 2.25% in the same snapshot. The divergence shows that investors were distinguishing between companies rather than selling every technology stock indiscriminately.

The broader weakness comes as investors question the cost of building AI infrastructure and the returns companies can generate from that spending. Nvidia's latest earnings beat expectations, but uncertainty following Jensen Huang's resignation has continued to weigh on the semiconductor giant.

Anthropic also faces an expensive expansion. Its IPO disclosures detailed approximately $900.9 billion in infrastructure and computing commitments extending through 2045, alongside another $150 billion to $175 billion in estimated payments under less precisely defined arrangements.

"Anthropic's record-breaking IPO has failed to rekindle enthusiasm for tech stocks," Joe Maher, market economist at Capital Economics, told Reuters.

Nvidia's weakness was notable given its latest results. The chipmaker reported $115.8 billion in quarterly revenue on Tuesday, up 103% from a year earlier, and forecast stronger-than-expected sales for the following quarter.

Even those numbers failed to erase concerns over the departure of longtime CEO Jensen Huang after allegations of extramarital affairs and possible leaks of corporate secrets and the sustainability of the AI spending boom.

The pressure also reached companies that rent out computing capacity. Neocloud operators CoreWeave and Nebius fell 5.0% and 7.8%, respectively. Software companies were weak as well: Salesforce declined 3.17% and Adobe lost 2.03% in the afternoon heatmap. From chips and data centers to enterprise software, the losses extended beyond any single corner of the AI trade.

Anthropic's IPO prospectus shows how closely these companies are tied together. Nvidia and Google each committed roughly $10 billion to a conditional private share placement alongside the IPO.

AMD agreed to invest $2.5 billion; Broadcom, Micron and Microsoft committed $1 billion apiece; and TSMC pledged $500 million. The $26 billion placement is separate from the public offering. Several of these investors are also key suppliers or infrastructure partners in the AI ecosystem.

That creates a central question for investors: How much of the money flowing into AI companies will ultimately translate into profitable demand for chips, cloud capacity and software?

Anthropic's blockbuster debut demonstrates demand for its shares, but Thursday's broader decline shows that Wall Street is not ready to extend that confidence to every company financing or supplying the AI boom.

#4992. CAT puts century-old train tech to work in its biggest underground machine yet

Diesel-electric locomotives have been barreling along America’s wide-open spaces for generations, and the century-old combination of highly efficient diesel engines spinning up generators to power high-torque electric motors has proven tough to beat. Now, Caterpillar is putting that century-old concept to work underground. Meet the CAT R3200 XE LHD.

One of the many hard-working machines moving chunks of Earth under your feet, an LHD (load, haul, and dump) machine is essentially a massive underground wheel loader designed to scoop up blasted rock, haul it through narrow mine tunnels, then dump it into trucks or ore passes. Built low and wide to fit in the tunnels, LHDs are workhorses of underground mining operations – and the new R3200 XE is CAT’s biggest yet, with a 25 ton payload and electric drive.

Before we get into the machine’s specs (the few that we have, anyway), I want to make sure understand that large-scale mining operations use obscene amounts of fuel, and a swing in site efficiency of just 1-2% can mean a huge difference in the bottom line – and fuel prices were up 27.4% (!) in August alone.

Keep the staggering weight of what that kind of fuel cost can mean to a fleet that buys fuel by the literal truckload as you read the rest of this.

Though not yet officially released by CAT, snippets of the company’s launch video have been leaking through dealers and trade journals, and they show the big machine powered by CAT’s newest 18.1 liter Tier 5 C18 diesel generator making 527 hp (~390 kW). That C18 reportedly sends electrons to the same electric drive system used in the company’s already successful 18-ton R2900 XE LHD.

In addition to a bigger generator and heftier payload, CAT says the upcoming R3200 XE LHD offers reduced cycle times versus the R2900 XE with 11% better speed on grade, plus reduced maintenance and repair costs thanks to design refinements for better durability, including redesigned axle. All told, that works out to 28% more tons per hour with 8% better fuel efficiency.

That efficiency is boosted by the same baked-in ADAS tech that’s made the smaller R2900 XE a favorite, and includes the latest version of CAT AutoDig and MineStar, ensuring that the machines are easy for experienced CAT operators to set up for remote, semi-autonomous, and even fully autonomous operation using Command for Underground.

We’ll post an update once CAT makes the full rundown of official specs public, which should be sooner rather than later. When that happens, we’ll see exactly how this big burrowing CAT stacks up against the competition from Sandvik, Epiroc, and Komatsu. In the meantime, let us know what you think of CAT’s newest electric drive machine in the comments.

#4991. In Jordyn Woods-Towns’s NYC Home, Every Day is Knicksmas: “The Whole House Is Knicks-ed Out Already!”

The most wonderful time of the year holds a special place in Jordyn Woods-Towns’s heart—and no, we’re not talking about the start of basketball season. The fashion designer got engaged to Knicks phenom Karl-Anthony Towns on Christmas Eve 2025, and after a whirlwind 2026 including an NBA championship win for the New York NBA team (possibly courtesy of her viral accessory-turned-amulet) and a clifftop wedding replete with stunning details, the couple can’t wait to create festive memories as husband and wife.

“This is my first married Christmas,” Woods-Town tells AD. “I’ve only been married three months, but it’s our first holiday season, so I definitely need to try to figure out what our new traditions are.”

The newlywed reveals that she created an entire PowerPoint presentation to prep attendees for her bachelorette party, so you’d best believe she appreciates a little organization when it comes to getting in the spirit for big days. Planner that she is, Woods-Towns linked up with design marketplace Minted for her first family Christmas card and a curated suite of picks to welcome one particularly merry and bright yuletide season of life. Below, AD gets her take on holiday colors, basketball-themed decor, and more.

In anticipation of the holiday season, Woods-Towns teamed up with Minted to curate a selection of festive stationery and decor.

Architectural Digest: Have you always been a big holiday person?

Jordyn Woods-Towns: Every single season, I decorate. On Valentine’s Day I have the girls over to do a charcuterie board with salami roses and chocolate covered strawberries. Karl and I went crazy for Halloween; we turned the entire front yard into a whole different space with a graveyard and a 20-foot-tall skeleton. On Christmas, I love a theme.

For a couple years I went with a Candy Cane Lane vibe and now I’m in my chic New York era. I love a Ralph Lauren Christmas. I love the natural linen and natural materials. I’ve been really into natural florals, textural things. I love feathers, incorporating some ostrich feathers throughout—I do a lot of that with my brand, and I feel like feathers are really having a moment right now.

In New York it’s been hard because I don’t drive and I don’t have my car. I can’t just run down to HomeGoods, grab something, and come back!

What’s your decor looking like this year?

I’ve been really into all one shade. There were a lot of greens in our wedding and green is my color of the season.

Woods-Towns is leaning toward florals and green for holiday decorating this year.

The tree’s already green. It could be kind of cool, full green-on-green. Now I’m the Grinch. [laughs]

With your Christmas Eve engagement last year, the holiday is a sweet part of your love story. What sorts of traditions are you looking forward to starting with Karl?

I started with the holiday card with Minted. This is our first holiday card as a family. Obviously after you have kids, it kind of changes, but right now we’re at a time where life is just… he has a [Christmas Day] game and so we’re like, “Okay, we’re living the young, fast life.” But as time goes on, as our marriage goes on, we’re going to build different traditions. We love to be with our family and I always cook every holiday, so I’ll definitely be cooking after the game.

Is there a signature dish you like to serve?

Karl’s a picky eater. He loves chicken, so some version of chicken. He’s never had beef or pork or anything in his whole entire life. It’s just us, so some type of chicken and sides. Pretty simple.

I wanted to use a photo from our wedding that really felt like us, something that not everyone has seen, to tie in our whole year. It was a green marbled border design with gold foil border by Jenna Holcomb. There are those shades of green, since there’s a lot of green incorporated into our wedding. Olive is very timeless, and it felt chic and like us, like something that people could keep. I don’t want to say everyone’s going to want to put a photo of us in their house, but I know our family [will].

The Towns family’s holiday card. The design is “Marbled” by Jenna Holcomb.

Are you hosting bigger parties this season or just keeping it more intimate with the celebrations?

No huge parties, just because I don’t have the capacity to do that right now, but definitely getting the family together. We don’t have a huge family, so it should be pretty intimate, hopefully doing something with the team getting together. I think one of the girls was talking about doing a holiday party—even though I love to be the host, I don’t mind just showing up.

I would say it’s all in the details. I think through everything. But overall, it’s about the vibe that you’re bringing, the energy, and what you’re putting out. People remember the music, the food, and how they felt.

It’s been a busy 2026 for Woods-Towns between then-fiancé Karl-Anthony Towns’s successful championship run with the New York Knicks and her August wedding, but she’s keeping her energy high heading into holiday party season. “I feel like there’s an event every other day. But it’s not going to be like this forever. I had to change my mindset from, ‘Wow, I’m so tired,’ to, ‘Wow, I’m so lucky to be able to do this.’”

Are you planning on sprinkling any Knicks Easter eggs throughout your home decor or in your gifting this year?

There’s so many Knicks things in my house that it’s hard to escape. It’s already everywhere, the whole house is Knicks-ed out already! But I don’t mind Knicks-themed gifting—people love the Knicks.

Karl’s very hard to gift for, and his birthday’s actually right before the holidays. So it’s hard to figure out two really good gifts in a short amount of time. Gift giving is one of my love languages, and I love getting people things that they really can utilize in their everyday life. I need to think about that.

How else do you get in the holiday spirit at home?

I already bought Christmas pajamas and I already watched The Grinch twice with my niece and nephew two days ago. So I’m ready!

#4989. Citi Says Customers Are Responsible When AI Banking Agents Go Rogue—Even After a Hack

Citi Says Customers Are Responsible When AI Banking Agents Go Rogue—Even After a Hack

Citi has updated its online banking terms to make customers responsible for the actions of third-party AI agents accessing their accounts, including when an agent leaks their credentials and someone else uses them to get in.

The change, reported by TechCrunch Wednesday, makes explicit how the bank intends to handle an increasingly awkward question: Who pays when software handling your money makes a mistake?

Under Citi’s new terms, actions taken using credentials supplied to an outside agent are treated as authorized by the customer, even if the tool ignores instructions, exceeds its permissions, or shares those credentials with another party.

Citi says it has no obligation to investigate whether the agent followed the customer's original prompts, subject to applicable law.

A Citi spokesperson told TechCrunch that the November revision clarifies the risks of sharing banking credentials or granting outside tools account access. The provision does not apply to AI agents offered by Citi itself.

Citi is not acting alone. JPMorgan and Bank of America announced similar policies in October, while Citizens Bank warned customers this week by email that they could be responsible for what their AI assistants do.

PNC also changed its digital agreement on Wednesday. Its rules distinguish bank-approved connections, which can provide limited access, from handing an agent unrestricted access to an account.

The move follows a banking security scare from October 22. Major banks had detected AI agents logging into customer accounts, sometimes taking steps that appeared to go beyond their users' instructions, and executives said they struggled to determine which agents had been properly authorized.

An AI agent differs from a conventional chatbot because it can act on a user's behalf, potentially navigating websites, accessing financial records, or initiating payments. That makes a mistaken instruction or compromised login more consequential than a bad answer about a bank balance.

The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency has since issued AI examiner guidance that addresses outside agents, payment controls, and human approval. The framework is nonbinding and does not itself create new requirements for banks.

Citi's language does not automatically eliminate consumer fraud protections. Under U.S. federal consumer protection rules, banks generally must investigate unauthorized electronic transfers and limit customers' financial liability for fraud. Those protections cannot simply be waived through a banking agreement, although their application to transactions performed by customer-authorized AI agents remains less clear.

The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau says banks cannot use agreements to waive those legal protections, although the rules distinguish theft by an outsider from transfers actually authorized by a customer or someone given access.

Whether a particular AI-related loss qualifies as unauthorized depends on how the transaction occurred.

PNC's updated agreement takes a stricter operational approach: Customers may use certain connection methods approved by the bank, but cannot give third-party AI agents their passwords or one-time security codes, and agents generally cannot initiate payments unless PNC expressly permits it.

#4988. Polestar unveils Formula 2030 concept, previewing the next Polestar 2

Polestar has now fully unveiled the Formula 2030 concept, a low four-door electric sports car that previews the design of the next-generation Polestar 2 coming in 2027 and the Polestar 7 compact SUV.

The concept sits just 1,350 mm (53 inches) tall, which is lower than the Polestar 5 grand tourer, and it brings physical buttons back into the Swedish brand’s interior.

We reported in September that Polestar confirmed the Formula 2030 concept after showing it privately to investors and retailers in Gothenburg. Now we get the full set of pictures and the details.

It’s the first show car built under head of design Philipp Römers, who joined from Audi in 2024.

Polestar calls the Formula 2030 a “compact practical four-door sports car” that “sits within its own segment.” It’s 4,680 mm (184.3 inches) long and 2,021 mm (79.6 inches) wide, on a 2,780 mm (109.4-inch) wheelbase.

For context, that’s about 3 inches longer than today’s Polestar 2 and roughly 5 inches lower. It’s also a bit shorter than a Tesla Model 3 and sits 3.5 inches closer to the ground. Polestar says the concept lands “somewhere between” the upcoming Polestar 2 and Polestar 7 in size.

The proportions are classic sports car: long hood, short overhangs, the cabin pushed back over big rear haunches, and 22-inch center-lock wheels. There are gold Brembo calipers behind those wheels and Öhlins dampers on display in the trunk.

Up front, Polestar kept its “Dual Blade” headlights, now set into an aero wing over a shark nose and a deep splitter. The automaker says this is the face of the next-generation Polestar 2 planned for 2027.

There’s a single vertical windshield wiper, like on a race car, and a LiDAR unit that hides under an aerodynamic shroud and only shows itself when the car is driving autonomously.

The rear is where things change the most. Polestar dropped the full-width light bar, which is on just about every EV these days, for what it calls “Single Blade” rear lights. It says they are being introduced here “ahead of series production.”

Römers described the concept as a “bold evolution” of the brand’s existing design:

“It is a physical embodiment of how we apply Polestar’s core values of design, performance and sustainability to the next production cars.”

The rear doors are hinged at the back and there’s no B-pillar, so the whole side opens up to four individual seats.

The interior is built around the driver. A curved 20-inch display, which Polestar calls the “HyperDIM,” is mounted directly on the steering column, and a 12.2-inch center screen sits in the center tunnel.

But the bigger news is below that screen. Polestar added a panel of eight physical controls for the most-used functions, and owners could swap between types of controls, like rocker switches or rotary knobs, and program what each one does.

Polestar says it is “committing to rebalance the mix of physical and digital.” Juan Pablo Bernal, the company’s head of interior design, put it plainly:

“As a performance brand, we see a renewed focus on the driver, and so we re-balance the digital and physical. We introduce physical buttons and controls.”

That’s a big change for a brand whose recent cars run almost everything through the center touchscreen.

The cabin also physically changes with the drive mode. There are three of them: Performance, Normal, and Autonomous. In Performance, the center screen drops flush into the console and the steering wheel and its display pull closer to the driver. In Autonomous, the wheel and the seat move away from each other.

The four seats use inflatable bolsters that shape themselves to each occupant, and the seat backs are made of a flax-based composite instead of virgin plastic. Google Gemini is built in, like in Polestar’s production cars.

The cargo area is the strangest part of the car. The rear opens as a clamshell, and the trunk floor is transparent, with custom Polestar bags strapped down underneath it with gold straps.

Up front, the frunk holds two race helmets and a fire extinguisher, framed by a gold strut brace.

Now for what’s missing. Polestar didn’t release a single powertrain spec. No battery size, no range, no power output, and no price. This is a design study, and Polestar isn’t saying it will build it.

What it does say is that “various design attributes” from the concept will show up on the next Polestar 2 in 2027 and the Polestar 7 in 2028. Those are two of the four new models Polestar plans to launch in three years, and the 7 is going to be built in Europe.

Europe is where this matters, since Polestar is shut out of the US under the federal connected-vehicle rule. The concept made its debut during the media drive of the Polestar 4 SUV.

Polestar always impresses me with its design, and this is no exception with this new head of design.

The proportions are sharp. Long hood, cabin pushed back, big haunches, and a roofline lower than the Polestar 5’s on a car with four doors and four real seats. If the next Polestar 2 keeps even half of this stance, it’s going to be the best-looking car in its segment.

I have loved Polestar from the day they launched. Every car they design is a work of art and I love their commitment to transparency and sustainablitity. The 2023 Polestar 2 is still one of my favorite cars I've ever owned. I've driven the 3 and the 4 and both were fantastic. The fit and finish, ride and build quality, and NVH were all excellent. The upgraded 3 was probably going to be my next car in 2027 until they were forced to withdraw from the US. I think their future with the new 2 and 7 are bright and I'm still hoping (though I'm not holding my breath) that they will return to the US at some point. If the 5 was available here, I'd buy it today.

I don’t know about the trunk of this thing. Polestar itself calls the rear “UFO-esque,” and between the wraparound glass, the clamshell and the see-through floor, it’s a lot. But everything else on this car is pretty sharp.

Polestar is putting physical controls back in its cars and saying so in plain words. The way they talk about it makes it sound like you can expect that of upcoming production vehicles.

Now the usual caveat. A concept car doesn’t fix a balance sheet. Polestar lost $842 million in the first half of this year on a negative gross margin. Design has never been Polestar’s problem. Building these cars and selling them at a profit is.

#4987. 9 Best Small Sectional Sofas That Are Truly Stylish (2026)

A sprawling living room might be the dream, but having a small space doesn’t preclude you from being able to stretch out on the couch. Sectionals specifically designed for smaller rooms prove that cozy movie nights and afternoon naps aren’t reserved exclusively for those with a massive floor plan. In fact, choosing a sectional with the right proportions stands to make a smaller room feel larger. There’s no reason to settle for a hodgepodge of chairs and ottomans when a thoughtfully selected sectional can transform every seat into the best seat in the house.

Being mindful of a space’s dimensions is always important when shopping for furniture, but especially so with a small room, where every inch may matter. Still, a variety of clever configurations—including L-shaped sectionals designed to nestle into corners, modular designs that are easily rearranged, and sofas with reversible chaises that give you more flexibility—cater to seemingly every layout. Add in performance fabrics, washable slipcovers, and supportive cushions, and you’ve got a recipe for some seriously comfortable yet compact lounging. Ahead, we’re sharing our favorite sectionals for small spaces that ensure every square foot counts.

The best-selling Abisko sectional from Article is made even more beautiful by colorful, performance velvet upholstery. Suitable for those with little ones and pets running around, the fabric is non-absorptive, meaning spills and crumbs won’t stay embedded in its weave. Two orientations—chaise and L-shaped—allow you to Tetris its silhouette into your space as you see fit.

Instead of opting for a giant L-shaped sectional that will take up the entire room, aim for something with a smaller footprint. Available in performance fabric and three leg finishes, this sectional couch is ideal for a tiny living space and a major upgrade from a smaller loveseat thanks to the chaise addition. While not an official fold-out sleeper sofa, the back cushions flop back to give you enough space should you be inclined to nap. Contributor David Kaufman, who tested it out for us, calls it “a great starter sofa for a first home or apartment that you won’t have to send to a landfill when you’re ready to move.”

Similar to the Thuma sectional contributor Evan Russum told us “feels solid and durable,” the Essential Sofa follows the brand’s signature simple-but-considered aesthetic with a minimalist silhouette,rounded cushions, and a grounded wooden base. Raised armrests add sculptural presence without overwhelming a small living room, while the detachable ottoman lets you switch between a left- or right-facing chaise—so everyone can have a turn on their favorite side of the sofa.

Not your average grey couch, AllModern’s Jossa sectional is minimalist in looks but generous on comfort, thanks to its dense foam padding that offers plenty of support without feeling stiff. Easy to de-assemble, the modular design allows the sofa to evolve with your seating needs. Craving two separate lounge chairs? Done. Prefer a love seat? Just slide the two larger seats side-by-side. Today’s layout doesn’t have to be tomorrow’s.

The slim arms and low profile on this this reversible three-piece sectional make the Unwind especially suitable for a limited living area as it doesn’t monopolize the space. Five neutral color variations all come in a linen blend, but olive’s grounding tones are speaking most to us. This sectional, like many of the others on this list, can be configured to be left-facing or right-facing depending on your living room setup, and we particularly like that in case you tend to switch up your design layout (we certainly do).

At just 62 inches wide, Sabai’s Essential Loveseat Sectional demonstrates how even the smallest living rooms can accommodate a proper chaise lounge. The compact design features clean lines, a generously sized chaise, and supportive foam cushions, offering the ideal spot to stretch out after a long day. Adding to the sectional’s appeal is its focus on sustainability. It combines a frame made from wood certified by the Forest Stewardship Council (FSC)—a third-party verification that ensures ethical wood sourcing—with upholstery fashioned from recycled natural materials. It’s also easy to clean and maintain, largely thanks to its washable slipcovers, sold separately—a welcome feature for anyone whose couch often doubles as a dining chair for meals eaten over the coffee table. Suffice it to say, this sectional is particularly well-suited to apartment living.

CB2’s Deseo sectional brings a little drama to small-space living, courtesy of rich, praline-brown performance velvet, broad arms, and a low-slung silhouette that practically begs you to sink in and stay awhile. The three-piece configuration, matching ottoman, and option for an extra-deep seat only extend the lounging possibilities and allow you to take advantage of every inch of your space. If brown doesn’t fit your space’s palette, worry not; the Deseo comes in plenty of other glamorous colors, including seven other performance velvet upholstery options.

Serious lounging is the goal for Sundays’ Movie Night sectional, with oversized cushions, deep seats, and a relaxed silhouette that makes it difficult to resist the urge to spend the afternoon totally horizontal. The cream linen upholstery adds to its laid-back feel, while the movable ottoman lets you stretch out or create a more open seating arrangement when company comes over. The company’s own LiveLife performance fabric is stain-resistant, moisture-repellent, and washable, with removable slipcovers that make living with a light-colored sofa significantly less intimidating.

Interior Define takes customization very seriously, and the Sloan sectional showcases how having such options can pay off in a small living room. Choose your preferred upholstery, cushion fill, seat depth, and leg style, then fine-tune the dimensions to suit your floor plan. The reversible chaise adds another layer of flexibility, allowing you to change its orientation, in case you rearrange your furniture or move to a new place with a different layout.

Contributor Malia Griggs tested the Sloan in her own 196-square-foot living room, where she found that its supportive cushions, tailored silhouette, and carefully selected dimensions worked beautifully alongside a narrow entryway. “If you enjoy tailoring your décor to your taste, are willing to pay a bit more for quality, and have the patience for a made-to-order process, this is a wonderful sectional—especially for a smaller space,” she added.

What Features Should I Look for in a Sectional for Small Living Rooms?

Modular furniture—any sectional that comes in several parts so you can adjust your sofa to suit the configurations—is built with flexibility in mind, making it the ideal contender for a small living space. We have tested and loved Castlery modular sofas, but a search for modular sectional should give you plenty of other options. A room tight on space can benefit from couches with storage, like those from Albany Park. Now you’ll be able to minimize the clutter and extra blankets by stowing them underneath your seat.

How Do I Arrange a Sectional in a Small Space?

Don’t fall for the tiniest sectional you can find, but rather invest in something well-made—it plays a big part in your living room, after all. While it may seem counterintuitive, Nashville interior designer Amanda Khouri says, “Filling a small room with small furniture can make it feel…well, smaller.”

Designer Alicia Murphy used a sectional in the living room of a teensy trailer she converted into a plush family getaway in Montauk, New York, for this very reason: “If you use a corner sectional rather than a sofa and chair, you most likely will add seating for two or three more people,” Murphy explains, noting that the alternative prevents you from having about 36 inches of dead space in the corner.”

Another way to make it work? Set an L-shaped sectional across from two club chairs to create a conversation zone, advises interior designer Suzanne Dawson.

What Do I Look for in a High-Quality Sectional?

When you’re working with a small space, quality counts. It’s much harder to get away with a mid-century modern knock-off when it’s one of four furniture pieces packed into the room. When shopping for a sectional, evaluate the materials and care instructions. Avoid anything with plywood, and polyester when you can. Seek out solid wood construction, such as walnut, oak, or teak; and premium fabrics, like linen, leather, or chenille. You’ll also want to keep the warranty and return policy in mind, in case you want to send back a piece that doesn’t work for you.

#4985. Lucid says service wait times fell 20% after 40% jump in service staff

Lucid (LCID) says service wait times dropped 20% globally in the third quarter after it grew its technician and service-support staff by more than 40% in a single quarter.

The automaker is also adding Studio and Service Centers in Southern California, Los Angeles, Dallas, and the Chicago suburbs, plus 20 more Gravity Mobile Service vans. It’s a clear sign that service had become a problem for Lucid owners.

Lucid announced the numbers today, a day after its Q3 2026 earnings. Both comparisons are against the second quarter, not a year ago.

The hiring isn’t done either. After a 40%-plus increase in technicians, advisors, and concierges in Q3, Lucid wants that figure at 50% by the end of 2026 and 60% by Q1 2027. Mobile Service capacity in North America grew 15%, with a 40% target for year-end.

That’s a big hiring push for a company that laid off 18% of its workforce in June, its second cut in four months after a 12% reduction in February. Roughly 1,500 people left across those two rounds.

And owners noticed. On the LucidOwners forum, one Air Touring owner posted in early October that Lucid told them in writing to expect “a service time of about 7 weeks” at its Beverly Hills Service Center. Other threads blamed service-department layoffs for slow repairs and recall work.

Billy Hayes, Lucid’s Chief Customer Officer, said the company is “adding service personnel, and increasing Mobile Service capacity to reduce wait times and provide more convenient, responsive support.”

Here’s what’s opening, according to Lucid:

Lucid is also letting a growing number of its Certified Collision shops handle recall campaign work, which should take some pressure off its own Service Centers.

Outside the US, the expansion leans on partners. Munsterhuis Autobedrijven is Lucid’s first retail partner in the Netherlands (Hengelo), Cloppenburg Automobil SE opens a Duisburg retail and service site in January 2027, Autohaus Possögel starts authorized service in Naumburg, Germany, in December, and Emil Frey France will support Lucid’s launch in France. In Saudi Arabia, Lucid opened its first company-owned Body & Paint Repair Center in Riyadh, with more service sites in Riyadh and Dammam coming in the first half of 2027.

Lucid doesn’t say what the average wait time actually is.

A 20% drop from seven weeks is still more than five weeks. A 20% drop from one week is a non-issue. Without a baseline, owners can’t tell which one they’re getting.

It’s also hard to separate better service from fewer cars coming in. Lucid delivered 3,806 vehicles in Q3, down 7% year-over-year, while it worked through inventory. Its fleet keeps growing, but slowly.

For context, Rivian delivered 19,248 vehicles in Q3, five times Lucid’s volume, and it’s been leaning hard on mobile service too. Lucid is a much smaller operation trying to cover the US, Europe, and the Middle East with a thin network.

This is the right move, and it’s overdue.

Lucid has been one of the few EV startups with genuinely class-leading hardware. The Air’s efficiency is still unmatched and the Gravity is a great vehicle on paper, even if we found its software wasn’t ready. But when you’re asking someone to spend $80,000 or more on a car from a brand with an uncertain future, the ownership experience is half the sale. A seven-week wait for a repair kills that sale, and the referrals that come after it.

So growing service staff by 40% in a quarter is a big deal. It also tells you how thin those teams had gotten after two rounds of layoffs. Lucid cut too deep in the wrong place, and it’s now hiring to fix it.

The problem is the timing and the money. Lucid burned $1.04 billion in free cash flow in Q3 and only stays funded into late 2027 because the PIF just added another $1.75 billion. Meanwhile, the Midsize “Cosmos” that’s supposed to bring real volume doesn’t start production until the second half of 2027. Service is exactly where Lucid should spend between now and then, because the buyers it has today are the ones who’ll decide whether anybody trusts the brand with a cheaper EV.

#4984. Ledger CTO Charles Guillemet to leave after nine years at company

Guillemet helped establish Ledger’s Donjon security lab and says his departure has been planned for months.

Ledger chief technology officer Charles Guillemet announced he will be leaving the company at the end of 2026, after nine years at the company.

In a post on LinkedIn on Thursday, Guillemet said he joined as chief security officer in December 2017, around three years after Ledger was founded. He launched Ledger Donjon, the company’s attack lab, a year later.

“We’ve been preparing this transition for many months, so Ledger’s teams, partners and roadmaps are ready. I’m bullish on Ledger’s future,” said Guillemet.

Guillemet has been a central figure in Ledger’s security operations, first as chief security officer and later as chief technology officer. He helped establish the Ledger Donjon attack lab, which tests hardware and software vulnerabilities. According to Guillemet, Ledger devices now secure roughly 20% of the world’s crypto assets.

“The threat landscape changed too. AI is making attacks cheaper, faster and easier to scale,” he added.

“The question we spent a decade answering for crypto (how do you protect what matters when any device can be compromised?) is now a question for every company, every AI agent and every government.”

Guillemet did not disclose details of his next venture but said he was “building something new” and would “dedicate my time to solving this security mess.”

Guillemet’s announcement comes weeks after Ledger disclosed that attackers had modified genuine hardware wallets with hidden components designed to capture users’ recovery phrases, and slipped the devices into authorized resellers.

The tampering cases were initially reported in Asia, with subsequent incidents identified in Europe and the United Arab Emirates.

#4983. CryptoUK Urges FCA Not to Treat DeFi Devs as Regulated by Default

CryptoUK Urges FCA Not to Treat DeFi Devs as Regulated by Default

The UK's main crypto trade association has called on the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) to make sure that developers and governance participants in decentralized finance protocols are not treated as regulated firms by default.

CryptoUK set out its position in a response to the FCA's consultation paper CP26/36, which proposes guidance on the "perimeter" of the UK's new crypto regime: which activities fall inside it and need FCA authorization, and which don't. The group, which says it represents more than 150 crypto companies, submitted its response on Wednesday, November 18, the day the consultation closed, and published it a day later.

Yesterday, CryptoUK submitted its response to the Financial Conduct Authority’s Consultation Paper CP26/36, which proposes amendments to the Perimeter Guidance Manual (PERG) to reflect the FSMA 2000 (Cryptoassets) (Miscellaneous Amendments) Regulations 2026.

The consultation… pic.twitter.com/oOrZgAWscP

— CryptoUK (@CryptoUKAssoc) November 19, 2026

"Software development, maintenance, security work and participation in decentralised governance should not, by themselves, establish that a person carries on a regulated activity," CryptoUK wrote. That would be consistent with the FCA's "clear controlling person" approach to DeFi, under which regulation should hinge on who effectively controls a financial service, it argued.

CryptoUK said it "broadly" supports the draft guidance, which reflects further amendments to the UK's crypto legislation that the government laid in September. The FCA aims to publish its final guidance in January 2027. It welcomed new exclusions from the regime for temporary settlement and payment arrangements, assets backing UK-recognized stablecoins, proprietary trading and market making, and technical service providers.

But in several places, the draft "goes further than the legislation," the group said. It pointed to a proposed link to the UK based on where a protocol is developed or governed, requirements in the exclusions for payments and proprietary trading, and indicators that would narrow the exclusion for technical services. The FCA has acknowledged that the timing of the latest amendments created uncertainty for some firms, and said it will give applicants extra time where questions over the technical services exclusion held up their applications for authorization.

The group asked the FCA to publish a public record of stablecoins that qualify under the UK regime, to clarify how stablecoins differ from electronic money, and to include more examples of activities that typically fall outside the perimeter.

CryptoUK also urged the FCA to raise with the Treasury outcomes that put UK firms at a disadvantage, citing the treatment of UK technical providers that offer access to regulated overseas trading venues, and of payments using stablecoins issued abroad. The UK should align with the EU's MiCA framework "where appropriate," it said. The response was prepared with law firm CMS and signed by CryptoUK policy director Nick Brooks.

The consultation is part of the FCA's work to build out the UK's crypto rulebook. The regulator finalized its core rules for crypto firms in June, ahead of a regime due to take effect on October 25, 2027, and later issued guidance two weeks before its authorization window for crypto firms opened. It has also set out a shared vision for tokenization with the Bank of England.

#4982. Institutions pile back into US Bitcoin ETFs in Q3 after selling streak

Asset managers added the equivalent of 49,229 Bitcoin to their US Bitcoin ETF holdings in the third quarter, reversing three quarters of net selling.

Institutional investment managers’ holdings of US Bitcoin exchange-traded funds climbed to a record high in the third quarter, as they reversed three straight quarters of net selling, according to regulatory filings.

The 13F filings, analyzed by Galaxy Research, show that the reporting companies added an equivalent of 49,229 Bitcoin (BTC) in the third quarter, outpacing the 47,054 Bitcoin they shed over the last three quarters combined. This lifted the reported total holdings to 356,491 BTC, the highest on record.

“The quarter’s accumulation was the work of a few dozen large institutions,” wrote Galaxy’s head of firmwide research Alex Thorn.

Quarterly 13F filings provide a point-in-time snapshot of US-listed securities held by reporting institutional investment managers. Thorn said half of the net addition of spot Bitcoin ETF shares came from advisors and wealth platforms.

Wells Fargo posted the largest increase, adding the equivalent of 14,636 Bitcoin, making it the largest institutional holder of spot Bitcoin ETPs. Other strong gainers included Brevan Howard, Bank of America, Millennium Management and Jane Street.

Largest holders of spot Bitcoin ETP positions in Q3. Source: Galaxy Research

“Early readings suggest longer-term holders make up a growing share of the spot Bitcoin ETF investor base,” Bitwise analyst Camran Khosravi previously told Cointelegraph, when the first batch of 13F filings had begun to come in.

The number of managers reporting a position in a spot Bitcoin ETF also rose for the first time in three quarters, increasing by 191 to 2,166.

This all came as Bitcoin gained about 43% in the third quarter, ending September at $83,621.

Related: Bitcoin ETF assets fall to three-month low as 2026 net outflows top $2.5B

Meanwhile, Galaxy’s data shows BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust accounted for the largest share of holdings reported by 13F filers, with the equivalent of 232,453 BTC held by the filers. This was followed by the Fidelity Wise Origin Bitcoin Fund.

Together, the two funds were responsible for 77% of all Bitcoin held by the reporting entities.

Bitcoin equivalent held by 13F filers. Source: Galaxy Research

The record institutional holdings in Q3 contrast with more recent weakness in US spot Bitcoin ETFs, with net monthly outflows reaching $515 million in October and $2.9 billion of outflows month to date, according to TFTC’s Bitcoin ETF tracker.

Earlier in the month, Bitwise head of research André Dragosch told Cointelegraph he viewed the selling as “related to a short-term risk-off environment rather than a structural change in institutional sentiment.”

#4981. Anthropic’s $81B IPO draws half the net retail buying of SpaceX’s

Retail investors traded $772 million in Anthropic shares on Thursday, the most Vanda Research has recorded for a market debut since 2012.

Retail investors traded $772 million in Anthropic shares on its Nasdaq debut Thursday, but their net purchases totaled just $60 million, about half the $118 million they put into SpaceX on its first day of trading in June.

Anthropic’s first-day retail trading volume topped SpaceX’s $669 million and was the highest for any market debut in Vanda Research’s data, which go back to 2012, Yahoo Finance reported.

Volume counts both purchases and sales, while net buying measures how much purchases exceeded sales.

The Claude AI developer and its existing shareholders offered 980 million shares at $83 each in the $81.34 billion initial public offering (IPO). Anthropic shares opened on Nasdaq at $111.50 on Thursday, 34.3% above the IPO price, and closed at $97.17 for a first-day gain of 17.1%.

SpaceX shares gained 19.2% in their June 12 debut, closing at $160.95 against an IPO price of $135, according to Nasdaq. Although Anthropic’s base offering exceeded SpaceX’s initial $75 billion sale, SpaceX ultimately raised $85.7 billion after underwriters exercised their option to purchase additional shares.

Before the IPO, Vanda forecast about $250 million in net retail buying, more than four times Thursday’s total. Its forecast drew on retail trading in past market debuts and the volume of Anthropic perpetual futures traded on decentralized exchange Hyperliquid.

Shortly before Nasdaq trading began, those futures traded at $110.48, just 0.9% below the stock’s opening price.

#4980. Unit1 FARO and NEON review: I just found my new favorite e-bike helmets

I test a lot of electric bikes, which means I also spend a lot of time wearing bicycle helmets. And while most helmets tend to fall into the decidedly unexciting category of “necessary safety equipment,” UNIT 1 has managed to make a couple that I actually get excited about wearing.

I’ve been using both the UNIT 1 FARO and the new NEON, and despite taking fairly different approaches, they’ve both become regular go-to helmets for me.

The FARO is the more futuristic-looking of the two, and it’s also the one that really leans into the “smart helmet” concept.

The helmet includes MIPS protection to reduce rotational impact during a collision, as well as integrated lighting on both the front and rear, including a large customizable rear lighting area made up of dozens of LEDs.

That large rear LED array is a feature I particularly appreciate since visibility is such a major part of cycling safety.

A helmet obviously can’t force drivers to pay attention, but I’d rather give them as many opportunities as possible to see me. The hidden light area below the obvious LED light bar adds a lot of extra visibility.

You can see just how vivid it is in the GIF below, though in real life it looks even better!

The FARO’s lighting system works with UNIT 1’s handlebar remote, which adds turn signals controlled right from the bars.

The system can also provide automatic brake-light functionality, giving you another way to communicate with traffic around you.

I’ll admit that turn signals on bicycles can sometimes feel a bit gimmicky, especially when they’re so close together that drivers can’t really tell which direction is flashing. But putting them high up on the helmet makes them considerably more visible, and the little wireless handlebar remote makes operating them incredibly easy.

The rechargeable lighting is also convenient. I’ve topped up the helmet from a power bank while out and about, meaning you don’t necessarily need to find a wall outlet if you realize your helmet is running low. The rear LED light bar also turns green and illuminates along the length of the bar to let you know what percentage of charge the battery has reached. The only way it could be clearer would be with a screen, but we’re still talking about a helmet here, not a phone.

There are other smart features packed in too, including crash detection and app-based customization.

The tradeoff is weight. At around 640 grams for a medium, the FARO is noticeably heavier than a conventional bicycle helmet. It doesn’t bother me much once I’m riding, and I’ve found the helmet comfortable, but you definitely know there’s more helmet up there. Each time I pick it up, I’m reminded that it’s not just the basic little foam shell that I’ve been wearing for the last few years.

Then there’s the price. At around $230 (or $195 during the current Black Friday sale period), this isn’t a cheap helmet. You’re paying for all of that technology, lighting, and design.

As much as I like the FARO, I’ve also become a big fan of the UNIT 1 NEON.

At roughly 430 grams in a medium, it’s significantly lighter than the FARO, and that difference is immediately noticeable. It’s also a bit cheaper at around $210 (or $178 during the Black Friday sale period) while still packing several of the smart features that make UNIT 1’s helmets interesting.

You still get MIPS rotational protection, crash detection, integrated rear lighting, app connectivity, and compatibility with UNIT 1’s handlebar remote for turn signals and brake-light functionality.

I do wish the NEON had a front light like the FARO. That’s probably the biggest feature I miss when switching between the two. But the NEON makes up for it with one of my favorite features on either helmet: its magnetic face shield.

The shield is ridiculously easy to attach and remove. You don’t even need to carefully line it up. I just need to get it somewhere near the mounting points with one hand and the powerful magnets basically grab it out of the air and snap it into position.

That means I can easily add or remove it one-handed, even while riding.

The photochromic shield is clear enough for night riding but darkens when exposed to bright sunlight, giving you sun protection without requiring separate daytime and nighttime shields. I’ve found that incredibly convenient, especially on rides that transition from daylight into evening. I hate that I can’t wear my sunglasses for eye protection at night, and a lens like this solves that issue.

The NEON also gets something particularly important for faster e-bike riders: NTA 8776 certification. That’s the Dutch standard designed specifically around higher-speed e-bike uses at up to 45 km/h (28 mph). For the Class 3 e-bikes that have become increasingly common in the US, that’s a big distinction compared to helmets rated for crashes at slower speeds.

That’s actually difficult, because I regularly use both.

The FARO is the one I’d choose if maximum visibility and technology were my priorities. I love having LEDs both front and rear, the MIPS protection, and the handlebar-controlled turn signals. It’s comfortable, looks great, and has become one of my favorite urban riding helmets.

But the NEON may be the easier helmet to recommend to most e-bike riders.

It’s lighter, a little cheaper, still gives you a rear light and smart safety features, has that excellent magnetic photochromic face shield, and importantly carries NTA 8776 certification for faster e-bike riding.

Neither helmet is inexpensive, and the FARO in particular asks you to accept some extra weight in exchange for all that technology. But I’m used to wearing much heavier motorcycle helmets and ways.

Plus, it’s important to note that these aren’t helmets I tested for a few rides and then tossed onto a shelf. Both have stayed in my regular rotation, and I find myself reaching for them frequently when I head out on an e-bike. The fact that I not only enjoyed them during my testing but actually replaced my old helmets with them should speak for itself.

For someone who rides as much as I do, that’s probably the strongest endorsement I can give them.

Between solid helmets like these and safe riding clothing, it’s good to feel protected!

#4979. After a Year of Washes, These Towels Are as Plush and Absorbent as the Day I Got Them

Utah-based bedding, bath, and loungewear brand Cozy Earth has built a $100 million business around bamboo. The brand is perhaps most loved for its luxe sheets, but we’ve also tested (and generally loved) its pajamas, blankets, and cotton-and-bamboo towels. In fact, most of our shopping team owns at least one Cozy Earth product, regarding them as “ultrasoft pieces that will reign forever in our linen closets,” as senior shopping editor Nashia Baker puts it.

The brand’s bamboo sheets have taken best overall in both our bamboo and cooling sheets roundups. Its towels have earned their own spots in our guides on the most absorbent bath towels, the best quick-dry towels, and the best waffle towel sets. Contributor Megan Wahn was sold on the waffle bath sheets after dunking a corner in a bowl of water: “I could literally see as the parts of the towel that were not submerged soaked up the water,” she says.

Towel marketing tends to promise softness and absorbency in the same breath, but in my experience, it’s rare that both are true. Cozy Earth’s Luxe Bath Towels are the exception. After a full calendar year of countless showers, followed by washing in New York City laundromats, where the dryers have one setting (and it’s “inferno”) they are still exceptional towels.

The feel was memorable from the start: plush and not the least bit scratchy. At 600 grams per square meter (GSM), a unit of measure for a towel’s weight, it also has real heft. The towel’s blend of cotton and bamboo viscose, woven using what the brand calls zero-twist technology, leaves no fabric loops for your hand to catch on. But despite lacking the shag-carpet texture of some fluffy towels, this soft, smooth Cozy Earth model remains absorbent enough to dry you with ease.

A year later the most impressive quality of these towels is how little they’ve changed. They’ve been through more showers than I can count and a year of intense washes (the care label calls for tumble drying on low, an option my laundromat doesn’t offer), and they’re still as soft to the touch as when I first got them. Plenty of cotton towels demonstrate their best absorbency in their first months, and then never again. The Cozy Earth Luxe towels still dry me off as well as they did on day one, which is something I can’t say for most towels I’ve owned (and I’ve tested a lot of them). In my experience, plush towels go stiff and absorbent ones go thin, but these have done neither.

The one concession to the laundromat is color. My off-white pair of towels has picked up a faint blue-gray tint over the year, though they still pass for white. For this I blame the machines more than the towels, which deserve better care than I can give them….

At $118 (currently $88.50 for Black Friday), I won’t pretend the Luxe Bath Towels set isn’t an investment. You can buy a 12-pack for the same price on Amazon. But these are my favorite bath towels due to their durability as much as their feel—a luxe combination that’s hard to replicate on a tight budget. Towels that stay soft and absorbent for a month are easy to find; it’s much rarer for options to hold their quality for a year and beyond. If you’re replacing a full bath-towel set, I recommend starting here instead of cycling through cheaper towels that end up costing you the same once you’ve replaced them a few times.

To outfit the whole bathroom, Cozy Earth sells the Complete Luxe Bath Bundle. The hand towels and washcloths are just as good as the towels.

#4978. Coinbase Targets In-House Prediction Markets by First Half of 2027: Report

Coinbase Targets In-House Prediction Markets by First Half of 2027: Report

Coinbase is planning to launch its own prediction market contracts in the U.S. in the first half of 2027, as it looks to take more control of one of its fastest-growing businesses.

The exchange plans to offer the in-house event contracts to both retail and institutional customers, Bloomberg reported on Thursday, citing a person familiar with the matter.

A Coinbase spokesperson told Bloomberg the company had "nothing new to announce today," and pointed to plans it set out in October to expand its prediction markets and improve their economics by building its own clearing and other infrastructure. The spokesperson did not address the timing of an in-house launch.

Coinbase rolled out prediction markets across the U.S. through a partnership with Kalshi, after unveiling the product alongside stock trading last year. Offering its own contracts would give Coinbase more say over which markets it lists, and let it keep more of the revenue from trades.

The exchange has been laying the groundwork for its pivot. In December 2025, it agreed to buy prediction markets startup The Clearing Company, and in September 2026 it received approval from the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) for its own clearinghouse. Coinbase already runs a regulated derivatives exchange.

Prediction markets have become a bright spot for Coinbase as crypto trading slows. The business passed $200 million in annualized revenue in the third quarter, with daily traders up more than 60% from the previous quarter, and revenue growing 82% a quarter on average since launch, the company reported in October.

"Prediction markets are adding another revenue stream and are less correlated to crypto volatility," CFO Alesia Haas said at the time. On an analyst call the same day, Haas said Coinbase's new clearinghouse meant it "can launch our own contracts, and we can also then earn better economics," while continuing to offer contracts through partners such as Kalshi. Asked when, she said: "We have not shared a timeline."

The products have faced legal challenges from states that argue some event contracts amount to unlicensed gambling. Coinbase sued three states over their attempts to regulate prediction markets, and New York sued Coinbase and Gemini over their offerings in April.

Last week, a Louisiana judge temporarily barred more than 30 prediction market providers, including Coinbase's derivatives arm, from offering event contracts in the state, after Attorney General Liz Murrill sued them on November 12, Forbes reported. The CFTC has sued Louisiana in federal court to block the order, and a hearing on a longer injunction is set for November 30.

Decrypt's parent company, Dastan, operates its own prediction market, Decrypt Predict.

#4977. SEC charges 8 firms over fake crypto platforms tied to $37M fraud

Fraudsters allegedly used social media ads, chat groups and forged SEC filings to defraud US investors of approximately $37 million.

The US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) charged eight Colorado-based entities with defrauding US investors of more than $37 million.

The defendants allegedly lured investors by masquerading as investment advisers or representatives of crypto asset trading platforms, which the SEC described as fronts designed to steal investor money, the agency announced in a Thursday press release.

The SEC said individuals overseas likely operated the entities and used social media ads to lure investors into private chat groups. They first offered stock-trading advice before persuading victims to transfer money to fake crypto platforms, where victims believed they were buying genuine crypto assets. The perpetrators created fake SEC certificates and submitted filings with the SEC, FINRA and FinCEN to feign legitimacy.

The SEC previously warned investors that scammers used investment-related group chats to promote fraud schemes, including by impersonating financial professionals, according to a December 2025 alert.

The scheme allegedly operated through four successive adviser-platform pairs from August 2024 to May 2026, with operators switching pairs every few months.

The eight entities charged were Advisor WeChat Capital, Tech Brokerage Asset Alliance Ltd., HB Wealth Advisors, IdeaCrypto Exchange LLC, Convergent Wealth Advisors Inc., RealSimple Crypto Exchange Inc., Associated Wealth Advisors Ltd., and Essential Crypto Exchange.

“The SEC continues to seek out and expose fraudulent investment scams that prey on U.S. investors,” said Laura D’Allaird, chief of the SEC Enforcement Division’s Cyber and Emerging Technologies Unit, encouraging the public to report such schemes through its online portal.

During fiscal year 2026, the SEC filed 348 enforcement actions, down 23.7% from 456 a year earlier. The SEC filed 13 crypto-related actions in calendar year 2025, down from 33 in 2024, according to Cornerstone Research.

#4975. BlackRock’s IBIT loses record $541M amid Anthropic market debut

BlackRock’s IBIT posted its largest daily outflow on record, taking three-session outflows near $900 million as BTC dipped amid a broader market selloff.

US spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds (ETFs) recorded $582 million in net outflows on Thursday, led by a record withdrawal from BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT).

IBIT posted $541 million in outflows on Thursday, its largest single-day withdrawal since launching in January 2024, according to Farside Investors data. The figure surpassed its previous daily record of $528.3 million, set on Jan. 30, 2026.

IBIT shares closed Thursday at $35.08, down 0.8% for the session. The shares have fallen 24.2% over the past month and 29.4% year to date, according to Yahoo Finance.

Thursday marked IBIT’s third consecutive trading day of outflows, totaling nearly $900 million. The latest streak followed a single day of inflows on Monday, which ended 11 straight sessions of withdrawals totaling roughly $2.35 billion.

The selling brought US spot Bitcoin ETFs’ November outflows to $3.47 billion, pushing their 2026 net withdrawals to approximately $3.11 billion, according to SoSoValue data.

Bitcoin (BTC) traded at around $61,875 at publishing time, down 3% over the past 24 hours, according to CoinGecko. The crypto asset was down 9.8% over the past seven days.

The ETF withdrawals coincided with a broader market selloff Thursday, as Anthropic’s highly anticipated stock market debut failed to sustain gains in AI-related stocks, including Nvidia, amid concerns over high valuations and heavy spending on artificial intelligence.
