#4974. Tesla’s China sales crash 66% to lowest level in over four years

Only 8,817 of the cars Tesla delivered from Giga Shanghai in October went to Chinese buyers. That’s down 66% from a year ago and Tesla’s worst month in China since July 2022, according to CPCA data.

Back in July 2022, the Shanghai factory was partly shut down for line upgrades. This time it ran normally and shipped 87% of what it built out of the country.

The China Passenger Car Association (CPCA) reported that Tesla China wholesaled 67,829 vehicles in October, up 10.3% year-over-year. That’s the number most headlines ran with.

But 59,012 of those were exports. Strip them out and you’re left with 8,817 cars for the domestic market, the one Giga Shanghai was originally built to serve.

Nearly all of them were Model Ys (7,807), according to CnEVPost, leaving just 1,010 Model 3s. And compared to September, when Tesla sold 64,837 cars in China, domestic sales fell 86%.

Here’s how October has looked over the last three years:

Tesla favors export orders early in each quarter and pushes domestic deliveries toward the end of it, and September’s promotions and quarter-end rush pulled some demand forward.

That’s real. Tesla’s China sales have followed this sawtooth pattern for years. Last October was also weak, and Tesla then delivered 73,145 cars in China in November and 93,843 in December.

But it doesn’t explain the size of this drop. Here’s every first month of a quarter in 2026:

October is less than half of the previous low this year. And the October trough keeps getting deeper: 40,485 in 2024, 26,006 in 2025, 8,817 now.

China’s EV market is having a rough year. NEV retail sales fell 10% year-over-year in October to 1.148 million units, according to CPCA’s preliminary data, as Beijing phases out trade-in subsidies and the NEV purchase tax exemption was cut in half on January 1. The overall passenger car market was down 25%.

Tesla was down 66%. That works out to about 0.8% of China’s NEV retail market last month.

Meanwhile, Xiaomi, which only started delivering cars in 2024, delivered more than 50,000 vehicles in October. Leapmotor delivered 106,127, up 51%. BYD delivered 490,168, though that includes its exports.

Through October, Tesla has sold 389,905 cars in China. That’s down 15% from 458,710 over the same period last year and its lowest January-to-October total in at least four years:

The decline is speeding up. Tesla was down 11.9% in China through September, and one bad October pushed that to 15%. This year is now 22% below the 2024 peak, or about 110,000 fewer cars.

Exports from Giga Shanghai went the other way, up 101% to 420,984.

So this year, Shanghai has now shipped more cars abroad than it sold at home. Last year, domestic sales beat exports by more than two to one.

As we reported last month, Beijing is cutting the VAT export rebate on EVs from 13% to 9% on April 1, 2027, with the rate set by the customs declaration date. We said to expect automakers to cram exports in ahead of the deadline. October’s 59,012 exports, up 66% year-over-year, fit that.

We’ve been tracking this gap all year, from Tesla’s Q1 China retail crash to the first-half numbers. Every time, the wholesale headline looks fine and the domestic number underneath gets worse. October is the most extreme version yet: Tesla China “grew” 10% while Chinese buyers bought 66% fewer Teslas.

We don’t buy that this is just the quarterly cycle. The cycle explains why October is weaker than September. It doesn’t explain why this October is a third of last October, or less than half of any other month this year.

I've been saying this for the last two years. Tesla's problem isn't that Elon temporarily alienated customers in Europe or other countries. Yes that killed sales for a bit, but in the end people are practical and will buy the best car for the money. And we saw that is exactly what happened with European Tesla sales coming back when gas prices rose and Tesla as a package (quality + price) was still very competitive.

The real problem that Tesla has is that they're falling behind in China not because anyone cares about Elon's politics, but because the cars are just less and less competitive. And while the Chinese competition doubles down on vehicle development and rolls out a new car every week, Tesla has lost all interest in it. There is absolutely nothing on the horizon for them in terms of new vehicles that consumers can buy. Looks like the 3 and Y are all they will have and no updates are coming.

I know, FSD or bust, but that's also assuming Chinese brands don't crack that nut at the same time.

Two things can be true at once. The export numbers show Tesla front-loading shipments ahead of the rebate cut. And Chinese demand for a Model 3 and Model Y lineup that hasn’t fundamentally changed in years keeps fading while Xiaomi, Leapmotor and BYD launch new models every few months.

And if Tesla is choosing to send cars abroad instead of selling them in China, that’s not exactly a vote of confidence in its Chinese business either.

The real test is November and December. Last year, Tesla bounced back to 73,000 and 94,000 domestic sales. If it gets close to that again, October was mostly timing. If it doesn’t, Tesla has a serious problem in the world’s largest EV market, and the export valve that’s been hiding it gets more expensive in April.

#4973. Bitcoin ETFs Shed $582M in a Day as BTC Drops Below $62K

Bitcoin ETFs Shed $582M in a Day as BTC Drops Below $62K

Bitcoin slid below $62,000 on Friday, extending a weeklong sell-off as investors pulled money from spot Bitcoin ETFs and braced for another interest rate hike from the Federal Reserve.

The leading cryptocurrency was trading at around $61,780, down 2.8% over the past day and 10% over the past week, after touching a 24-hour low of $61,273—its lowest level since early July—according to CoinGecko data. It has fallen more than $2,000 since struggling to hold $64,000 earlier this week, and has also formed a so-called death cross, a bearish chart pattern.

The drop triggered $727 million in liquidations across crypto markets over the past 24 hours, about 86% of which were long positions betting on higher prices, according to CoinGlass. Bitcoin accounted for just under $202 million of the total, with more than 151,000 traders liquidated.

Spot Bitcoin ETFs recorded $582.2 million in net outflows on Thursday, their largest single-day outflow since October 30, according to SoSoValue data. The funds have lost more than $1.1 billion so far this week and almost $3.5 billion in November, while their total net assets have fallen to $76.6 billion.

"Within crypto, the most telling sign is this month's outflow from spot Bitcoin ETFs, which suggests investors are choosing to stay on the sidelines for now," Neil Steinhardt, head of Nexo U.S., told Decrypt.

Treasury yields above 5% and expectations that the Fed will raise rates in December have weighed on assets that don't pay interest, including Bitcoin and gold, Steinhardt said. "Because the pressure appears tied to the rate backdrop, and that backdrop has shifted before, a turn in yields or the dollar would likely be the first signal that appetite is returning," he added, pointing to the December 4 jobs report and the Fed's December 9 meeting as the next checkpoints.

Fed Governor Christopher Waller has called for a larger, half-point increase at that meeting, unless policymakers signal another rise in January. Traders are betting on a smaller move: CME FedWatch puts the odds of a quarter-point hike on December 9 at 99.2%, with the chance of a half-point increase falling to almost zero from more than 9% on Thursday morning.

The decline has left the average Bitcoin holder only just in profit. Bitcoin is still trading above its realized price, the average price at which every coin on the network last moved, but the margin is thin, onchain analytics firm Glassnode tweeted on Friday. A break below would put holders in loss for the first time since early 2023, it said.

The average Bitcoin holder is still in profit.

bitcoin:native trades above its realized price, the average cost of every coin on the network. The margin is thin: MVRV sits just above 1.

A break below would put holders in loss for the first time since early 2023. pic.twitter.com/rPOTbZS1NF

— glassnode (@glassnode) November 20, 2026

CoinShares head of research James Butterfill sees the slide as part of a longer downturn. "I see this as a continuation of the existing bear market rather than the start of another," he said in a note published on Thursday, pointing to selling by large holders since late 2025, expectations of higher rates and weakness in tech stocks.

CoinShares' base case is for Bitcoin to trade between $60,000 and $90,000 through much of 2027, until falling inflation gives the Fed room to ease, Butterfill said.

#4972. Bitcoin nears repeat of chart pattern that preceded 2023’s $25K retest

Bitcoin’s 21-day moving average fell below its 200-day average, and analyst Keith Alan expects a second bearish crossover by Sunday.

Bitcoin (BTC) could repeat a pair of bearish moving-average crossovers that preceded its retest of $25,000 in September 2023, according to analyst Keith Alan.

New analysis from Keith Alan, cofounder of crypto trading platform Material Indicators, compares this week’s Bitcoin chart with a similar setup in 2023.

On Bitstamp’s BTC/USD daily chart, the 21-day simple moving average (SMA) crossed below its 200-day equivalent on Thursday. The move last occurred in early November 2025, around one month after Bitcoin’s latest all-time high of $126,200, in the early stages of the current bear market. The 50-day SMA crossed below the 200-day SMA later that month, forming a conventional death cross.

Alan expects the 50-day SMA to cross below the 100-day SMA by the end of the week.

“We’ve only seen this happen once before in Bitcoin’s history, and it should not be ignored,” he summarized in a post on X.

BTC/USD one-day chart with 21-, 50-, 100- and 200-day SMAs. Source: Cointelegraph/TradingView

The only other time in Bitcoin’s history that the two pairs of moving averages both produced a so-called “death cross” in the same period was between August and September 2023. BTC/USD retested support near $25,000 on Sept. 11.

Alan describes this double bottom as the start of a rally that took Bitcoin to its 2023 high of $44,700 in early December — an increase of 80%.

“One occurrence is by no means a large enough sample to consider a reliable pattern, or expect similar returns/drawdowns, however the timing, placement, and candle characteristics have enough similarities that we can’t ignore it either,” he said.

BTC/USD one-day chart with 21-, 50-, 100- and 200-day SMAs. Source: Cointelegraph/TradingView

Previously, Cointelegraph reported on Bitcoin losing support at the 200-week SMA for the first time since mid-August. The trend line typically functions as support during bull-market retracements, but it can act as resistance when Bitcoin rebounds from below it.

Related: Institutions pile back into US Bitcoin ETFs in Q3 after selling streak

BTC/USD fell to $61,231 on Friday, its lowest level since July 3, a day after Anthropic’s record IPO and Nasdaq debut. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index finished Thursday’s trading session down 2.25% at 23,879 points, its lowest daily close since April 14.

Anthropic shares traded around $91.50 before Friday’s open. It closed Thursday at $97.17, 20% below the day’s $115 peak.

#4971. 11 Best Dining Tables to Elevate Take-Out Nights (2026)

Even if you order takeout (almost) every evening, the best dining tables can make all of the difference for elevating your dishes, down to the cold leftovers you’ve reheated for dinner. You don’t have to be a regular hostess to know that these furniture pieces are more than a place to eat; they double as a surface to display your latest tableware finds, function as a desk, and even help facilitate conversation. Whether you’re looking to outfit a quaint breakfast nook or source something with panache for a formal dining area, the best dining tables bring in just the right amount of personality without distracting from what’s actually important—the people you’re eating with.

Ahead, we’re highlighting our 11 favorites, from a perfectly mod pedestal to an extendable farmhouse beauty. Looking for a dining table that was made for small spaces? We have options for you too.

Paired with the Meja dining chairs, Article’s Plumas table helped senior shopping editor Nashia Baker convert an empty living room nook into a dining setup. With slightly angular legs and rounded corners, the table evokes a classic, midcentury silhouette (fitting perfectly with the rest of Baker’s apartment aesthetic). The extendable feature is accessible simply by pulling a latch underneath the table and sliding either end apart. With the table pushed against the wall, she says her “current setup works just fine to comfortably seat three people.” Baker does plan on using the extendable design during larger holiday parties “so there’s plenty of space for a potluck-style tablescape.”

West Elm’s Miles dining table was the investment shopping producer Lauren Arzbaecher needed to fully maximize guest seating in her Brooklyn apartment. “I love playing host—poker nights, RuPaul’s Drag Race watch parties, you name it. An extendable table was an ideal solution to seat extra guests for a dinner party while not eating up extra square footage on a regular day,” she says. In the 60 to 80” size, Arzbaecher can sit up to 10 guests around the table (though it requires some squishing onto the matching bench). With a modern, rounded silhouette, the double-edge detailing along the sides of the tabletop perfectly complements the equally curvy dining chairs the producer already owned. And despite its substantial appearance, the table is surprisingly agile. “Don’t let the chunky look deceive you,” she says. “This table isn’t heavy, and I’ve been able to move the leaf in and out on my own with ease.”

With a vibe that falls somewhere along the spectrum of an upstate farmhouse and Spanish revival, this rectangular dining table from Green Row charmed commerce writer Julia Harrison with its extendable surface and rich wood stain. “This table does the work of modern design at its best: It looks completely authentic—like it was lifted from a small rural French farm, dusted off, and dropped in my dining room in Brooklyn,” she says. Extended, she notes that it comfortably fits eight people, and has paired it with some dark wood Windsor chairs to create an overall farmhouse-esque effect. “It's the sort of table that makes you want to host things, the way good writing can inspire you to write,” she adds.

Strikingly modern and architectural, the Aava dining table from Wayfair is the ideal budget pick for those still looking to make a major design impact. The perpendicular legs create a kind of futuristic aesthetic while the classic wood stain options (black, natural, and white) mean that this table can suit a number of design styles, from modern to minimal.

Pedestal tables boast timeless design appeal thanks to their streamlined build and versatile aesthetic (it’s part mod, part midcentury, part Scandi—this table fits anywhere). Architect Eero Saarinen was inspired to eliminate cumbersome legs from dining tables, and in doing so, he inspired countless dupes and recreations of his innovative round pedestal shape. Whether it’s just you in your apartment or a Thanksgiving-level gathering, this oval dining table offers a number of sizes to accommodate your friends and family. The sturdy, oval pedestal base ensures no drinks are spilled as you maneuver in and out of your seat, while the thin tabletop leaves ample room for all chair heights and seat positions.

For small apartment dwellers or those looking to finally stop eating meals on the couch, a space-saving bistro table is the way to go. This painted steel version from Schoolhouse, similar to a traditional pedestal dining table, is both durable and lightweight, offering plenty of room for a meal for two. The high-gloss finish is a dramatic (and welcome) reprieve from the traditional wood surfaces that characterize the genre.

Great for small dining spaces and eat-in kitchens, a drop-leaf silhouette offers a kind of versatility not seen in traditional dining tables. This best-seller from Pottery Barn has a rectangular frame with two sections that lower to create a smaller square for everyday use. The leaves also include additional supports that can lock into place for added stability.

It’s rare to find a stylish drop-leaf table, especially for those looking for a round option for their small dining area. This one from West Elm can collapse both sides to sit flush with the wall and save valuable floor space in small apartments (even the legs fold in). Extend one side only if it’s just you, or sit four dining chairs comfortably with a 42-inch diameter at full size.

Designed by fashion content creator Aimee Song, the Hannu round dining room table boasts a playful, bulbous shape. Made from fibercement (meaning it’s safe for both indoor and outdoor use), this table’s ivory finish and curved edges intentionally soften the materials' typically utilitarian applications.

Sculptural and dramatic, this marble dining table holds its own against any number of statement seating choices. The black and white veining gives off an Italian modernist feeling, but this table can easily shift between design styles depending on what you choose to pair it with.

As seen in the Hollywood Hills home of TV writer and producer Cameron Johnson, this CB2 dining table has a streamlined, Brutalist feel with its offset legs. This solid wood dining table is available in both 63 inches (best for seating four to six) and 91 inches (best for six to eight seats).

#4970. VanEck to end Gemini ETF custody deals, keeps Coinbase

VanEck plans to end Gemini’s custody agreements for three crypto ETFs in February 2027, while Coinbase will continue serving as a custodian for the funds.

VanEck is cutting ties with Gemini as a custodian across three cryptocurrency exchange-traded funds (ETFs), ending a relationship that began with its first spot Bitcoin ETF.

VanEck notified Gemini on Monday that it would terminate custody and clearing agreements for its Bitcoin (BTC), Ether (ETH) and Solana (SOL) ETFs, according to separate filings with the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) on Thursday.

The agreements will end “on or about” Feb. 16, 2027, while Coinbase Custody, which already serves the funds, will continue providing custody services.

The move raises questions about Gemini’s position in the US spot crypto ETF market, where Coinbase serves as custodian for many of the largest funds. The filings did not disclose the reasons for the terminations.

The termination extends beyond cryptocurrency custody. VanEck’s Solana ETF (VSOL) filing also covers a Gemini staking services agreement, raising questions about how the fund will handle staking after the transition.

Staking allows tokenholders to earn rewards by helping secure a proof-of-stake (PoS) blockchain such as Solana. For ETFs that stake their holdings, the service can provide an additional source of returns for the fund.

Cointelegraph contacted VanEck and Gemini for comment on the reason for terminating the agreements and the potential impact on the Solana ETF’s staking operations, but had not received a response by publication.

Gemini’s founders, Cameron and Tyler Winklevoss, were among the earliest proponents of spot Bitcoin ETFs in the United States, filing to launch the Winklevoss Bitcoin Trust in July 2013. US regulators did not approve the first spot Bitcoin ETFs until January 2024, more than a decade after the brothers’ initial filing.

Gemini became the original Bitcoin custodian for VanEck’s spot Bitcoin ETF when the fund launched in January 2024, before VanEck added Coinbase Custody in June that year.

Related: Gemini’s quarterly retail trading volume sinks to 3-year low

VanEck’s Bitcoin ETF (HODL) is considerably smaller than the largest US spot Bitcoin funds, holding about $880 million in assets under management, compared with $47.6 billion for BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT) and $10.6 billion for Fidelity’s Wise Origin Bitcoin Fund (FBTC), according to Wallet Pilot data as of Thursday.

Gemini has also provided custody services for crypto ETFs in Canada and Australia. In the US, it continues to serve as a custodian for at least one smaller fund, the 7RCC Spot Bitcoin and Carbon Credit Futures ETF (BTCK), which identified Gemini and BitGo as its Bitcoin custodians in a September 2026 regulatory filing.

#4969. MoonPay Applies for National Trust Bank Charter to Grow Custody and Stablecoin Business

MoonPay Applies for National Trust Bank Charter to Grow Custody and Stablecoin Business

Crypto payments firm MoonPay has applied for a U.S. national bank charter, joining a growing list of crypto companies seeking a federal banking license.

The proposed MoonPay National Trust Bank would be based in Miami Beach, Florida, according to the company's November 17 application to the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC), Bloomberg reported on Thursday. The charter would help MoonPay grow its custody business and expand its stablecoin services, according to the application.

MoonPay confirmed the move on Thursday, tweeting that it was "proud to share" that it had applied for a U.S. national bank charter with the OCC.

today we are proud to share that MoonPay has applied for a US National Bank Charter with the OCC 🇺🇸 pic.twitter.com/XGHBPx84v0

Unlike a full-service bank, a national trust bank can hold and manage assets for clients, but can't take deposits or lend money. The OCC did not immediately respond to Bloomberg's request for comment.

Founded in 2019, MoonPay is best known for providing on- and off-ramps between fiat currencies and crypto. It has been expanding into new areas including AI, having launched a crypto wallet designed for AI chatbots, let users buy crypto through ChatGPT, and acquired AI trading copilot startup Dawn Labs.

It has also been courting institutions. In April, it acquired Sodot, a Tel Aviv-based crypto key management firm, to form the basis of MoonPay Institutional, a unit serving banks, asset managers and trading firms. The unit is led by former acting Commodity Futures Trading Commission chair Caroline Pham.

MoonPay is the latest crypto firm to seek a federal charter under President Donald Trump's administration. Earlier this month, Coinbase joined Circle and Ripple in receiving final OCC approval for a national trust bank, after Ripple won approval for a trust bank behind its RLUSD stablecoin. Jack Dorsey's Block has also applied for a charter to custody Bitcoin, while World Liberty Financial, the crypto venture tied to the Trump family, won conditional approval for its own trust company in August.

The approvals have drawn pushback. A banking group has sued over Block's application, accusing crypto firms of seeking "side door" access to banking, while Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-MA) has argued that the OCC's approvals of Coinbase and Ripple were illegal, a claim the crypto industry has disputed.

Warren is expected to chair the Senate Banking Committee from January, and is expected to examine World Liberty's charter as part of a wider look at Trump-linked crypto ventures.

#4968. The coolest ride in town is England’s first electric ice cream truck

The “world’s leading ice cream truck manufacturer” has released its first fully electric ice cream truck, which is already in operaiton, and it says it’s open for orders for more.

Whitby Morrison bills itself as “the world’s leading ice cream truck manufacturer,” supplying converted vans as ice cream trucks to drivers worldwide.

And now it has taken a big step into the modern age delivering its first fully electric ice cream truck to Hocking’s dairy in North Devon, England.

The truck has been operating since July, through the course of one “ice cream season.” It reportedly covered more than 100 miles a day and has done days serving up to 12 hours at a time.

It’s built on a standard Mercedes eSprinter, so it’s not retrofitted from the diesel vans that make up most of Whitby Morrison’s other offerings. The eSprinter comes in a “chassis cab” configuration which comes with just the chassis and cab, and lets upfitters build whatever they want onto the back end of the vehicle.

In this case, it also got some pretty extensive (and a little over-the-top) art all around the vehicle, highlighting the van’s electric operation.

The ice cream truck maker, Whitby Morrison, says this is the “world’s first fully certified electric ice cream truck.”

We’re not sure what sort of international certifications are required for an ice cream truck so we’ll take their word for it, but we have seen a Rivian EDV turned into a Ben & Jerry’s ice cream truck, complete with side window, and a concept electric ice cream truck as far back as 2019. So it’s certainly not the very first time this idea has been had, at least.

And it is a good idea. As with school buses, ice cream trucks are vehicles that children are likely to congregate around. Having a stinky old truck spewing emissions just a few feet away from those kids’ lungs is the sort of thing that can expose them to a life of health problems… and we might as well not stack that on top of the sugar addiction we’re teaching them to have (hey, at least they have to get outside to chase the truck down, so they’re getting some physical activity out of it, right?)

It also opens up more possibilities for operators to serve at events where having a diesel truck running might not be reasonable, like in enclosed spaces or where quiet might be appreciated (this came up when we went to Harbinger Motors’ factory opening, where local food trucks were in attendance, inside the large factory building, and made the air quality noticeably worse).

Whitby Morrison says it’s taking orders both in the UK and overseas, with US orders just opening. To learn more, head on over to its website.
